p: This bill is a symbolic pro forma measure introduced before the Throne Speech
It asserts the Legislative Assembly's right to sit and act without Crown permission
It affirms lawmakers can give priority to matters other than those raised by the Sovereign
The practice traces back to at least 1558 and was codified by the House of Commons in 1604
It follows a tradition used in certain other parliamentary jurisdictions to mark the first bill's constitutional importance
Introduces measures to reduce interprovincial trade and labour barriers, including mutual recognition of goods/services, direct-to-consumer alcohol sales, and expanded labour mobility.
Also creates a new symbolic day promoting Ontario and Canadian purchases.

a.t: Buy Ontario, Buy Canadian Day Act, 2025
p: Declares the last Friday of June each year as Buy Ontario, Buy Canadian Day.

a.t: Fair Access to Regulated Professions and Compulsory Trades Act, 2006
p: Changes timelines for domestic labour mobility applicants from business days to calendar days.

a.t: Liquor Control Board of Ontario Act, 2019
p: Allows Minister to direct LCBO to implement a framework for interprovincial direct liquor sales.
Requires LCBO to comply with Minister's directives on this framework.
Adds new section allowing agreements with other provinces/territories to enable direct liquor sales to consumers.
Allows regulations to implement these agreements and govern related liquor sales.

a.t: Ontario Free Trade and Mobility Act, 2025
p: Lets Lieutenant Governor in Council designate other provinces/territories as reciprocating jurisdictions.
Goods from reciprocating jurisdictions to be treated as meeting Ontario standards, under conditions.
Service providers authorized elsewhere gain equivalent Ontario authorization, under conditions.
Includes liability protections and new regulation-making powers.
Bars out-of-province regulatory authorities from imposing extra prescribed requirements for certification.
Sets new timelines for Ontario authorities to respond to out-of-province certified applicants.
Creates one-time six-month deemed certification for already out-of-province certified individuals.
Adds offence for knowingly making false representations to meet certification requirements.
Amends the Gift of Life Act to allow public identification of deceased organ or tissue donors
Only the deceased person's name may be used, no other identifying details or transplant date disclosed
Identification must be for memorial or appreciation purposes as the hospital sees fit
At least six months must have passed since the transplant before public identification
Consent for public identification must be obtained from the person who gave or would give substitute consent
The short title of the Act is the Robbie's Legacy Act (Honouring Beloved Organ and Tissue Donors), 2025
Comes into force on the day it receives Royal Assent
Changes organ and tissue donation from opt-in consent to a presumed consent (opt-out) system after death
People 16 or older can object to tissue removal before death, in writing, orally with witnesses, or by recorded message
Parents or guardians must consent on behalf of children under 16 before tissue can be removed after death
Family members, in a set order (spouse, children, parents, siblings, next of kin), can object on behalf of someone who died without objecting
Hospitals and other designated facilities must notify Ontario Health when a patient dies or death is imminent
Ontario Health must create and maintain a registry recording people's objections or consents to tissue removal
Ontario Health's role expands to plan, coordinate and support tissue removal, donation and transplant activities

Bill 5 changes multiple Ontario laws to speed up mining, energy and development projects, restrict foreign-sourced goods/services in energy procurement, and replaces endangered species protections with a new species conservation framework.
It creates a new Special Economic Zones law letting the government exempt chosen projects and proponents from normal legal requirements, and repeals the Endangered Species Act, 2007.
Directives to IESO for procurement can now set requirements or restrictions based on geographic origin of goods, services, people or entities.
IESO barred from certain procurement contracts based on geographic origin conditions set by regulation.
New restrictions on Ontario Power Generation Inc. and its subsidiaries procuring goods/services based on geographic origin.
Extinguishes certain legal claims against the Crown, IESO, OPG and others connected to these amendments, and bars related lawsuits.
Changes the Act's purpose and several key definitions, including a new definition of 'habitat'.
Makes listing species under section 7 discretionary rather than mandatory, and removes temporary protections upon initial listing.
Repeals government response statements, management plans, hearings process, and the Species at Risk in Ontario Stewardship Program (renamed).
Removes warrant requirement for some inspections; replaces stop orders with contravention and mitigation orders; sets up wind-up of the Agency.
Terminates the agreement and revokes an approval related to the proposed Eagle's Nest multi-metal mine near McFaulds Lake.
Exempts specified activities at the Chatham-Kent waste disposal site from Part II.3 approval requirements.
Revokes a ministerial document that set fees for the Environmental Activity and Sector Registry.
Allows the Minister to refund such fees if a registration is removed from the Registry.
Purpose of the Act now ties encouraging mining/exploration to protecting Ontario's economy.
Minister may suspend mining lands administration functions or restrict/ban users, licences and leases to protect the strategic national mineral supply chain.
New mine authorization and permitting delivery team can coordinate and expedite permits across ministries for designated projects.
Minister, with Cabinet approval, can cancel mining claims, licences or leases for supply-chain protection reasons; related legal claims are extinguished.
New restrictions bar specified gas transmitters, distributors, storage companies and licence holders (and subsidiaries) from procuring goods/services based on country, region or territory of origin.
Extinguishes certain legal claims against the Crown and others connected to these amendments and bars related lawsuits.
Expands inspection powers to assess for artifacts or archaeological sites on land, ordered by the Minister; findings must be reported.
New assessment orders can halt alteration/removal of artifacts until archaeological fieldwork is completed.
Minister gains expanded seizure and deposit powers for artifacts, including deposit with Indigenous communities; new investigation powers with search warrants added.
New two-year limitation period for prosecutions and new court orders to address damage from offences; exemptions can be granted for specified provincial priorities with related claims extinguished.
Exempts proposals related to the Ontario Place Redevelopment Project from Part II of the Environmental Bill of Rights, 1993.
Enacts new law letting Cabinet designate special economic zones and Minister designate trusted proponents and projects.
Cabinet can exempt trusted proponents or designated projects from requirements under any Act, regulation or municipal by-law within a zone.
Cabinet can also modify how such laws or by-laws apply to a trusted proponent or designated project.
Extinguishes certain legal claims connected to these exemptions and modifications.
Enacts new Act replacing the Endangered Species Act, 2007, continuing COSSARO to assess and classify species.
Cabinet may list species as extirpated, endangered or threatened; certain federally-listed migratory birds and aquatic species are excluded.
Prohibits activities causing a species to disappear from the wild in Ontario, and requires permits or registration in a new Species Conservation Registry for specified activities.
Continues the Species Conservation Program for habitat preservation, public education and grants; sets rules for permits, enforcement, appeals and offences.
Creates a new law banning consumption of illegal substances in public places and giving police new enforcement powers, and adds sentencing factors for trespassing offences.

a.t: Restricting Public Consumption of Illegal Substances Act, 2025
p: Prohibits consuming an illegal substance in a public place, subject to specified exemptions.
Defines 'public place' to include structures like tents used as unlawful dwellings there.
Lets police or provincial offences officers order a person to stop, leave, or give their name and address.
Officers may seize, remove and destroy suspected illegal substances and arrest without warrant; fines up to $10,000 or six months jail, or both.
Adds two aggravating factors courts must consider when sentencing for the trespass offence.
One factor: defendant stayed on premises after being told to leave, even if they left temporarily.
Other factor: court finds the defendant likely to trespass again in the future.
Makes minor corrections and updates to the French version of the Act.
Requires health professionals to treat patients with fairness, not just sensitivity and respect
Makes charging patients an unfair fee for a service a form of professional misconduct
Allows discipline panels to order reimbursement of unfair fees and a three-month licence suspension
Requires Colleges' patient relations programs to include measures preventing unfair fees
Lets Council make regulations defining what counts as an 'unfair fee'
Allows the Director to revoke or suspend a health centre's licence for charging unfair fees
Restricts eliminating licensed services unless linked to unfair fee concerns
Amends the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997 to reclassify certain employers
Employers operating residential care facilities become Schedule 1 employers under the Act
This includes retirement homes, rest homes and senior citizens' residences
Employers operating group homes are also made Schedule 1 employers
Applies to both public and private employers in these industries
The Act takes effect six months after receiving Royal Assent
Short title is the WSIB Coverage for Workers in Residential Care Facilities and Group Homes Act, 2025
Changes how codes of conduct work for Toronto city council and other Ontario municipal councils, shifting rule-making power to the provincial Integrity Commissioner.
Creates a new process where local integrity commissioners can recommend a council member's seat be declared vacant, subject to review by the Integrity Commissioner of Ontario.
Lieutenant Governor in Council, not the City, may now prescribe the code of conduct for council and local board members.
Integrity Commissioner of Ontario must provide education and training to the City's Integrity Commissioner.
After an inquiry, the Commissioner may recommend to the Integrity Commissioner of Ontario that a member's seat be declared vacant.
If a vacancy is recommended, city council is required to vote on the recommendation.
Lieutenant Governor in Council, not municipalities, may now prescribe the code of conduct for council and local board members.
Integrity Commissioner of Ontario must provide education and training to municipal Integrity Commissioners.
After an inquiry, a local Commissioner may recommend to the Integrity Commissioner of Ontario that a member's seat be declared vacant.
If a vacancy is recommended, the municipal council is required to vote on the recommendation.

Bill 10 amends eight different Acts to strengthen public safety, bail administration, and the justice system, including new rules on sureties, sex offender registration, judicial appointments, motor vehicle theft devices, and illegal drug premises.
It also creates a new Act letting authorities target landlords who knowingly allow their properties to be used for drug production or trafficking.
Sureties and former sureties who become Crown judgment debtors must provide information as regulations require.
Crown Attorneys may now delegate their powers and duties under sections 1 or 7 of the Act.
More people can now apply for restraining orders on behalf of those already entitled to apply.
Clarifies that a rule on minor parents applies to those who have never been married.
Voyeurism under Criminal Code section 162 now counts as a 'sex offence' regardless of any court order.
Special in-person reporting rules for offenders against children apply even without federal registration duty.
Chiefs of police may request temporary policing assistance from entities governed by other Canadian jurisdictions' laws.
O.P.P. detachment boards must now participate in choosing a permanent detachment commander, per regulations.
Minister's complaints under sections 106 and 107 must be in writing.
Inspector General may impose interim measures when the Minister requests it, under set conditions.
New provincial judge candidates must agree not to request a transfer for five years, barring extenuating circumstances.
Restriction on appointing lawyers to the Judicial Appointments Advisory Committee is removed.
Committee's advertising, review and recommendation processes no longer need a specific judicial vacancy.
Committee must classify candidates as 'not recommended', 'recommended' or 'highly recommended' for the Attorney General.
More people can now apply for restraining orders on behalf of those already entitled to apply.
Prohibits possessing an electronic motor vehicle theft device intending to use it to steal a vehicle.
Such devices can be seized and are forfeited to the Crown after 30 days.
Provisions allow relief from forfeiture in certain cases.

a.t: Measures Respecting Premises with Illegal Drug Activity Act, 2025
p: Prohibits landlords from knowingly permitting premises to be used for drug production or trafficking offences.
Prohibits knowingly possessing proceeds from an offence under this new Act.
Specific offences covered will be set out later by regulation.
Includes enforcement provisions and lets authorities recover enforcement costs.
Bill 11 makes several changes to Ontario's health care laws, including new staffing agency reporting rules, digital health identifiers, and public health governance changes.
It affects the City of Hamilton's public health board, Connecting Care Act services, mandatory blood testing, and personal health information protections.
Establishes a separate board of health for the City of Hamilton.
Previously the City itself held all board of health powers and duties.
Applies the French Language Services Act to the Service Organization.

a.t: Health Care Staffing Agency Reporting Act, 2025
p: Requires staffing agencies to report aggregate billing and pay rate data to the Minister.
Requires agencies to maintain specified records.
Allows the Minister to publish certain reported information.
Creates offences and penalties for non-compliance with the Act.
Medical officers of health must notify and get written approval from the Chief Medical Officer before issuing a class order.
Allows nurse practitioners to perform many functions currently limited to physicians.
Creates a new Part V.2 governing digital health identifiers created by a prescribed organization.
Requires the prescribed organization to maintain privacy practices and notify individuals of breaches.
Gives the Minister power to issue directives to the prescribed organization.
Adds a new offence for disposing of records to evade an access request.
Increases the Ontario small business deduction rate from 8.3 per cent to 9.9 per cent
Raises the business limit for the small business deduction from $500,000 to $600,000
Adjusts the surtax formula for Ontario small businesses to match the new $600,000 limit
Changes take effect on January 1, 2026
Also known as the Cutting Taxes on Small Businesses Act, 2025
Creates the Primary Care Act, 2025, setting Ontario's vision for publicly funded primary care
Sets six objectives: province-wide access, connected services, convenient timing, inclusive and non-discriminatory care, empowered access to personal health information, and responsive system
Requires the Minister to publish an annual report on progress toward these objectives, starting within one year of the Act coming into force
Report must include the percentage of insured persons with an ongoing relationship with a primary care clinician or team
Clarifies the Act creates no private legal right, duty of care, or fiduciary duty for any person
States that failing to comply with the Act does not invalidate any related policy, law, regulation or decision
Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to make regulations detailing objectives, reporting information and how reports are published
Amends long-term care and retirement home laws to improve dementia care, add new offences, and strengthen protections for seniors.
Introduces new director roles, resident rights, and ministry powers concerning infectious disease management in care homes.
Licensees must have organized programs for dementia care and cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual needs.
New offences added, including for abuse or neglect of a resident.
Licensees guilty of an offence for contravening any Act or regulation provisions.
Medical Director role re-enacted as Clinical Director, allowing a physician or registered nurse in the extended class.
Adds a new resident right to ongoing support from caregivers under the Residents' Bill of Rights.
Allows senior ministry officials to give binding direction and recommendations on managing infectious diseases.
Declares October each year as Kids' Online Safety and Privacy Month in Ontario
Aims to raise awareness about children's safety and privacy while using the Internet
Highlights risks like cyberbullying, online grooming, exploitation and trafficking facing children online
Encourages parents to be educated and equipped to supervise children's online activities
Supports discussion of online safety in schools to inform children about risks
Takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Creates 150-metre access zones around religious institutions like churches, mosques, synagogues and temples
Bans advising, persuading or persistently asking people to avoid entering a religious institution within the zone
Prohibits intimidation, physical interference, threatening conduct or repeated following within the zone
Bans repeated phone, fax or electronic communications meant to dissuade someone after they ask it to stop
Sets fines up to $5,000 or six months jail for a first offence, higher penalties for repeat offences
Allows people who suffer losses from violations to sue for damages
Lets courts issue injunctions and lets police arrest offenders without a warrant
Amends eight Ontario laws to speed up building approvals, transit projects, and housing development, while adjusting municipal development charges and planning rules.
Expands provincial powers over transit and infrastructure projects and limits certain municipal restrictions on schools and building construction.
Restricts the Building Materials Evaluation Commission's powers in certain circumstances.
Repeals clause 29(1)(a) and makes related amendments to section 29.
Clarifies that municipalities cannot use certain Municipal Act or City of Toronto Act powers to pass by-laws on building construction or demolition.
Adds a definition of 'provincial transit project' and makes related changes.
Removes timing restrictions on when a portable classroom was placed on a school site for defining 'development'.
Sets new rules for information and material prepared by a person in a prescribed profession.
Exempts long-term care home developments from development charges.
Adds new circumstances where the standard by-law amendment process does not apply.
Allows residential (non-rental) developments to pay charges at occupancy permit issuance or first occupation, whichever is first.
Caps charges tied to Planning Act or City of Toronto Act application dates so they cannot exceed the standard section 26 amount.
Allows the Minister to direct municipalities or their agencies to share information and data for provincial transit or transit-oriented community projects.
Repeals section 7.1 and paragraph 2.1 of subsection 19(2).
Adds new section 10.1 letting the Minister direct municipalities to provide information, data and documents to the Minister or Ontario Infrastructure and Lands Corporation.
Revokes Ontario Regulation 378/24.
Restricts official plans and zoning by-laws from prohibiting elementary or secondary schools on urban residential land.
Requires Minister's approval before councils or planning boards make certain official plan amendments.
Sets minimum setback distances for buildings from parcel boundaries on certain lands.
Removes timing restrictions for portable classrooms in the 'development' definition and lets the Minister impose conditions in section 47 orders.
Expands the list of projects included in the definition of 'priority transit project'.
Removes the need for Lieutenant Governor in Council approval in certain circumstances and adds Ontario Infrastructure and Lands Corporation as a delegate.
Adds new section 4.1 on agreements necessary to support transit-oriented community projects.
Authorizes up to $197,120,171,300 in public service expenses for April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025
Authorizes up to $6,080,302,200 for public service investments in capital assets, loans and other investments
Authorizes up to $355,400,500 for expenses of Legislative Offices, including the Assembly, Auditor General and Ombudsman
Repeals the Interim Appropriation for 2024-2025 Act, 2023 and the Supplementary Interim Appropriation for 2024-2025 Act, 2024
Allows spending to be incurred by whichever ministry holds responsibility for a program during the fiscal year
Is deemed to have come into force on April 1, 2024, with the Act itself repealed starting April 1, 2026
Sets out detailed funding amounts by ministry in Schedules A, B and C
Amends the Health Protection and Promotion Act to set maximum patient-to-nurse ratios
Requires a 1-to-1 ratio for critical care patients on ventilators
Requires a 2-to-1 ratio for critical care patients not on ventilators and highly dependent mental health patients
Requires a 3-to-1 ratio for specialized care patients
Requires a 4-to-1 ratio for inpatient and palliative care patients
Requires a 5-to-1 ratio for rehabilitative care, except 7-to-1 on night shifts
Lets regulations set the required mix of nurse practitioners, registered nurses and practical nurses
Creates a new non-refundable tax credit for children's extra-curricular activities in Ontario
The credit can reduce tax owed by up to $1,000 per year
Applies to Ontario residents for taxation years ending after December 31, 2024
Cabinet may make regulations setting rules for administering the credit, including required receipts
The Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Taxation Amendment Act (Promoting Leisure Activities for Youth), 2025
Creates the Foodbelt Protection Plan Advisory Committee with members appointed within 60 days of Royal Assent
Committee members drawn from farmers, agricultural experts, soil scientists, planners and food/agricultural organizations
Committee will recommend a Foodbelt Protection Plan to preserve a continuous agricultural land base and reduce land speculation
Committee must consult broadly with the agricultural community and publish its report within 12 months of Royal Assent
Minister of Agriculture must report to the Assembly within 60 days of receiving the Committee's report
Amends the Planning Act to block rezoning or use changes on designated agricultural land without an Agricultural Impact Assessment
This assessment requirement applies to both municipal zoning by-laws and Minister's Zoning Orders
Declares the first full week of October each year as Ontario University Athletics Week
The Act took effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Official short title is the Ontario University Athletics Week Act, 2025
Requires care home landlords to itemize charges for care services and meals separately in agreements
Charges for care services and meals must match the landlord's information package and be the same for every tenant
Landlords must let tenants choose individual services from a package instead of paying for a bundle
Allows tenants and landlords to sign separate written agreements for extra care services or meals, which tenants can reduce or cancel with 10 days notice
Bans increasing care service or meal charges more than once every 12 months and caps yearly increases at the rent guideline percentage
Voids any charge increase that breaks these rules, with limited regulated exceptions capped at 3 per cent over three years
Requires retirement home operators closing down to tell residents they keep their tenant rights and that closure notice is not a termination notice
This budget-implementation omnibus bill amends 18 existing Ontario statutes and enacts two new ones, covering taxes, tolls, bicycle lanes, securities regulation and more.

Key changes include removing municipal power to run toll highways, restricting bicycle lane removal/restoration rules, raising securities and tobacco fines, adding new tax credits, and authorizing $27 billion in borrowing.
Sets standard rules for notices, including allowing electronic delivery by the assessment corporation.
Lets the assessment corporation share information for purposes the Minister prescribes by regulation.
Gives the Minister power to regulate how recipients disclose that shared information.
Makes consequential amendments to the City of Toronto Act and Municipal Act.
Removes the City's power to designate, operate or maintain any highway as a toll highway.
Repeals the related toll highway regulation-making power.
Bars the City from taxing individuals for issuing or validating certain Highway Traffic Act permits.
Lets CIRO's Chief Executive Officer appoint employees with investigative powers and confidentiality rules.
Shields current/former CIRO directors, officers, employees or agents from personal liability for good-faith acts.
Raises maximum court fines for violations from $5 million to $10 million.
Raises the maximum administrative penalty per violation from $1 million to $5 million.
Expands how the Minister may send assessment notices, including electronically or by other prescribed means.
Makes other minor housekeeping amendments.
Adds bond forward agreements as a type of investment the Minister of Finance may hold or enter into.
Removes propane from the definition of taxable fuel, since it is no longer taxed under the Gasoline Tax Act.
Sets a new tax rate for clear fuel.
Repeals various spent provisions.
Ends taxation of propane under the Act starting July 1, 2025.
Sets new tax rates for gasoline and leaded gasoline.
Corrects a French translation error and repeals spent provisions.
Repeals the Act entirely and makes consequential amendments to the Highway Traffic Act.
Requires the Minister to restore certain Toronto bicycle lanes for motor vehicle use by reconfiguring them.
Lets the Lieutenant Governor in Council order removal or reconfiguration of other existing bicycle lanes.
Bans municipal contracts that pay automated enforcement suppliers based on number of offences or revenue share.
Requires municipalities to publish locations of speed and red light cameras and post signage if regulated.
Lets the Lieutenant Governor in Council apply, clarify or exempt Provincial Parks Act provisions for historical parks.
Creates a new Historical Parks Account to record related Crown revenues and expenditures.
Allows amounts in the account to fund park expenses, refunds and reimbursements.
Reduces the basic tax rate on beer made by microbrewers, effective August 1, 2025.
Changes how a brewer's worldwide production limit is calculated for microbrewer status from March 2, 2026.
Cuts the basic tax rate on spirits from a distillery retail store from 61.5% to 30.75% of retail price, effective August 1, 2025.
Allows prescribed alternate tax rates for low-alcohol 'alcohol refreshment beverages' (up to 7.1% ABV).

a.t: Members of Executive Council Recognition Act, 2025
p: Creates a new Act allowing former Executive Council members to be designated Honorary Members.
Lets all Executive Council members, including honorary ones, use 'The Honourable' and 'E.C.O.' titles.
Removes municipalities' power to designate, operate or maintain any highway as a toll highway.

a.t: National Capital Children's Oncology Care Inc. Act, 1990
p: Adds a definition of 'specified property' and makes related housekeeping amendments.
Requires ministerial approval for all Corporation by-laws, not just financial ones.
Lets the Minister direct how the Corporation pays its net profits into the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Enacts a new Act authorizing the Crown to borrow up to $27 billion.
Lets CIRO's Chief Executive Officer appoint employees with investigative powers and confidentiality rules.
Shields current/former CIRO directors, officers, employees or agents from personal liability for good-faith acts.
Raises maximum court fines for securities law violations from $5 million to $10 million.
Raises the maximum administrative penalty per violation from $1 million to $5 million.
Requires repayment of the Ontario made manufacturing investment tax credit in certain new circumstances.
Creates a new refundable Ontario fertility treatment tax credit equal to 25% of expenses up to $20,000.
Adjusts eligibility and calculation rules for the small beer manufacturers' tax credit.
Increases the base or range amounts of fines under several offence provisions, with a new maximum additional fine.
Creates a new offence for possessing 10,000+ cigars or 100,000+ grams of other tobacco at a controlled site.
Extends that new offence to cover possession while in transit to or from such a site.
Overhauls Ontario's emergency management governance, redefining the roles of the Minister, a new Commissioner of Emergency Management, and various entities in developing emergency plans.
Gives the Minister of Community and Social Services new powers to direct and enforce compliance from funded entities during extraordinary circumstances.

a.t: Emergency Management and Civil Protection Act
p: Adds a purpose provision and replaces references to the Solicitor General with the Minister.
Re-enacts section 2 to set out the Minister's powers, including developing a provincial emergency management strategy.
Continues the office of the Commissioner of Emergency Management, who must establish an advisory committee and coordinate 'Ontario Corps' resources.
Removes the Chief, Emergency Management Ontario role and creates a provincial emergency management organization within the Minister's Ministry.

a.t: Ministry of Community and Social Services Act
p: Authorizes the Minister to issue directives to funded entities providing community and social services during prescribed extraordinary matters.
Allows the Minister to issue an order requiring compliance if an entity fails to follow a directive.
Establishes an offence for knowingly contravening a Minister's order.
Makes minor French-language corrections to subsection 9 (4) and clause 13 (1) (g).
Creates two new provincial park classes: Urban Class Parks and Adventure Class Parks
Urban Class Parks aim to improve access to nature-based recreation in or near urban centres
Adventure Class Parks support activities like rock climbing, tree-top trekking, mountain biking and off-road vehicles
Classifies Charleston Lake Provincial Park as an adventure class park
Classifies Uxbridge Urban Provincial Park as an urban class park
Allows the government to create further park classes and set their objectives by regulation
Requires adventure class park management plans to maintain existing compatible uses
Renames and updates wildland fire management rules, creates a new legal framework for storing carbon underground, and makes changes to oil/gas well safety powers and surveyor licensing.
Renames the Act to the Wildland Fire Management Act, replacing 'forest fire/area' with 'wildland fire/area'
Re-enacts section 4 to let the Minister appoint or designate fire officers with defined roles
Creates new permits for outdoor fires outside restricted fire zones during fire season
Requires certain entities to have a wildland fire management plan, and adds remediation orders and administrative penalties
Creates a new Act allowing carbon storage sites, defined as wells and underground repositories used to store carbon dioxide
Prohibits research, evaluation, and carbon storage activities unless done under a permit issued under the Act
Makes pore space rights part of surface property rights, but lets Cabinet vest them in the Crown by regulation with compensation rules
Establishes the Carbon Storage Stewardship Fund, funded by authorization holders, to cover closure and liability costs

a.t: Oil, Gas and Salt Resources Act
p: Gives the Minister power to act to prevent or reduce hazards to the public or environment from an oil/gas well or work
Allows the Minister to recover the costs of such action from the operator or from security funds the operator posted
Lets the Registrar issue limited and temporary licences, and allows retired members to be reinstated
Moves licence/certificate requirements like exams and experience rules into by-laws instead of the Act
Removes the requirement that regulations and by-laws be confirmed by member vote, and repeals the Fees Mediation Committee
Allows appeals of Academic and Experience Requirements Committee decisions to the Registration Committee, and permits service of notices by email or fax
Creates the Homelessness Ends with Housing Act, 2025 to guide efforts to end homelessness
Requires the Ontario government to design a strategy aiming to eliminate homelessness within 10 years
Sets strategy goals like better data collection, more deeply affordable rental units and supportive housing
Calls for increased funding to the Canada-Ontario Housing Benefit and a housing-first approach
Requires the Minister to create an 11-member Homelessness Advisory Committee within 90 days, including people who experienced homelessness
Requires an annual public report tracking numbers of unhoused people, deaths, repeat homelessness and available units
Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to prescribe extra information for future reports
Declares the first week of June each year as Extreme Heat Awareness Week in Ontario
Requires the Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks to publish extreme heat information on a government website
Website must cover preparation, prevention, health risks, resources and FAQs about extreme heat
Minister must mail this extreme heat information yearly to households in territories without municipal organization
Amends the City of Toronto Act to require extreme heat information be sent with tax bills
Amends the Municipal Act to require municipal treasurers to include extreme heat information with tax bills
Most requirements take effect three months after the Act receives Royal Assent
Bill 30 makes changes to labour, employment, and workplace safety laws, including new job posting rules, extended layoffs, and stronger penalties for workplace safety and insurance violations.
It also gives the province new powers to limit municipal and planning control over training and skills development projects.
New section lets the Lieutenant Governor in Council limit City powers over training or skills development undertakings.
Amends Act to reference Planning Act regulations on sections 113 and 114 for such undertakings.
Job posting platforms must let users report fraudulent job postings and have a written policy on them.
New job seeking leave: 3 unpaid days if 50+ employees are terminated together.
Extended layoffs allowed (35+ weeks in 52, but under 52 in 78) with employee and employer agreement plus Director approval.
New section lets the Lieutenant Governor in Council limit municipal powers over training or skills development undertakings.
Accredited health and safety management systems must be treated as equivalents.
Employers can be reimbursed for defibrillator costs.
New administrative penalty scheme lets inspectors issue penalty notices for violations.
Inspectors may require a person to attend a separate in-person interview during inspections.
Some regulation-making powers can be delegated from Cabinet to the Minister.
Training or skills development undertakings are exempted from the Act and from sections 113/114 of the City of Toronto Act.
Adds related regulation-making powers.
Prohibits employers from making false or misleading statements about a worker's benefits claim.
Adds administrative penalties under sections 80 and 89.
Contravening section 88 becomes an offence.
Repeat convictions in the same proceeding face up to $750,000 per count, with new aggravating factors for penalties.
Amends the Marriage Act to let members of the Legislative Assembly solemnize marriages under a licence
Members must give written notice to the Minister to gain this authority
The authority continues for 12 months after the person stops being a member of the Assembly
The Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Amends the Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act, 2016 to create a beverage container deposit program
Requires a deposit of at least 10 cents for containers one litre or less, 25 cents for larger containers
Defines 'grocery store' based on size, food product variety, and floor space rules
Requires grocery stores and Brewers Retail Inc. stores to act as collection depots for beverage containers
Requires these stores to refund the deposit to people returning beverage containers
Makes it an offence for Brewers Retail Inc. or grocery store owners to fail to comply with the collection depot and refund rules
Comes into force one year after receiving Royal Assent
Amends four Ontario Acts covering child and family services, education governance, and colleges/universities.
Expands Ministry oversight of school boards, sets new rules for children's aid societies, and adds accountability rules for post-secondary institutions.

a.t: Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
p: Re-enacts section requiring Ombudsman information be given in more circumstances, in language suited to the person.
Requires children's aid societies to review and update by-laws and make them public, per regulations.
New section 41.1 requires Minister's approval for financial transactions or arrangements affecting a society's approved budget.
Removes maternity homes from the exclusion in the definition of "institution" in section 62.
Allows Minister to direct investigations of a board's affairs over any matter of public interest, including duty performance.
Lets Minister give directions to boards and vest control and charge of a board in the Minister for non-compliance.
Adds Ministry auditors and internal auditors alongside existing external auditors and audit committees.
Requires boards to work with local police on school access, programs, and school resource officer programs; requires Minister approval for school names.

a.t: Ministry of Training, Colleges and Universities Act
p: New section 16.0.2 requires merit-based admission assessment and public disclosure of criteria for programs.
New section 20.1 requires colleges and universities to develop and implement research security plans.
New section 21.1 allows regulations governing fees charged to or required from students.
New section 24 makes this Act and its regulations prevail over conflicting Acts or regulations, with one exception.
Expands the Ombudsman's functions relating to services under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, with complementary amendments.
Removes the cap that limited MPP annual salaries to the 2009 level
Sets the Government House Leader's salary addition at 19.2 per cent
Ends membership in the old MPP pension plan for current members, effective 2026
Makes MPPs members of the Public Service Pension Plan instead, with special vesting rules for the 44th Parliament
Allows the government to create a new MPP supplemental pension plan by order, with terms set out in a schedule
Requires Board of Internal Economy consent before benefits or contribution rates in the supplemental plan can change
Lets MPPs choose how to transfer or use funds from their old pension account, with a statement due by February 1, 2026
Requires a licence to establish, operate or maintain a zoo in Ontario
Sets out application requirements including animal inventories, site plans and emergency plans
Lets the Registrar issue, refuse, suspend or revoke licences based on set conditions and grounds
Gives licensees the right to a hearing before the Director if a licence is refused, suspended or revoked
Requires annual inspections of zoos and allows inspectors to order fixes for violations
Allows removal of animals from unlicensed zoos and sets fines up to $50,000 for individuals and $250,000 for corporations
Gives existing zoo operators one year to get licensed and lets some current wild animal owners keep animals until they die
Adds a new Part IV.1 to the Occupational Health and Safety Act to address heat stress at work
Requires the Minister to create a Worker Heat Protection Standard within 12 months of the section coming into force
Standard must include engineering controls, work schedule adjustments, breaks and employer-paid protective equipment
Employers must create a Heat Stress and Protection Policy, do heat stress assessments, and review annually
Workers must have access to cool drinking water near work areas and get heat stress training
Employees must be paid their regular wage for rest breaks, medical removal and training time under the standard
Minister must report yearly to the Legislature on heat-related illness, deaths and enforcement for five years
Declares the fourth week in March each year as Flooding Awareness Week
Requires the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing to publish flood preparedness and prevention information on a government website
Requires a guide to flooding resources and FAQs about flooding risks in Ontario to be published online
Requires the Minister to mail flooding information yearly to households in territories without municipal organization
Requires Toronto's city treasurer to send flooding information along with tax bills to taxpayers
Requires municipal treasurers under the Municipal Act to send flooding information along with tax bills
Most provisions take effect three months after the Act receives Royal Assent
Proclaims September of each year as Ethiopian Heritage Month in Ontario
Recognizes contributions of Ethiopian Canadians to Ontario's social, economic and cultural life
References cultural events like Enkutatash, Maskel and Irreechaa celebrated in September
Act took effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Short title given is the Ethiopian Heritage Month Act, 2025
Restricts when Ontario bills can use the notwithstanding clause under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Allows its use only for urgent, temporary situations seriously endangering Ontarians' lives, health or safety
Also allows its use to amend a law a court found violated the Charter, limited to the specific provisions found in contravention
Requires the Attorney General to table a report justifying the clause's use within 30 days of the bill's introduction
Report must explain why alternatives to using the clause were considered inadequate
Requires a two-thirds majority vote of elected members to pass any bill invoking the notwithstanding clause

Amends three energy-related statutes to add economic growth as a policy objective, adjust electricity payment and connection rules, ease municipal utility franchise procedures, and update Ontario Energy Board powers and procurement rules.
Adds economic growth and hydrogen market development as new purposes of the Act
Expands Independent Electricity System Operator's objects to support economic growth
Allows certain generator, Financial Corporation and distributor payments to come from legislature-appropriated funds instead of market adjustments
New section bars transmitters or distributors from connecting or reconnecting certain load facilities unless regulatory requirements are met
Removes requirement for municipal electors to approve by-laws granting public utility rights or occupation of highways
Municipality now simply passes a by-law setting terms and conditions instead
Expands Ontario Energy Board's authority to also cover construction, extension or addition of gas distribution works, not just renewal
Pending applications before the Board continue under the amended Act; consequential amendment made to the Public Utilities Act
Adds economic growth as a new objective for regulating the electricity sector
Allows the Board's chief executive officer to issue internal policies on hearing procedures
Makes new Electricity Act connection rules enforceable and overriding Board orders, codes or licences
Adds new provision letting the Minister pay transmitters from appropriated funds, to be factored into rate-setting
Creates the 9-1-1 Everywhere in Ontario Act, 2025 to improve emergency call services across the province
Requires the Minister to ensure everyone dialing 9-1-1 connects to a call centre or local police service
Sets a December 2026 deadline for compatible computer dispatch systems allowing information sharing and caller location tracking
Requires an interoperable radio channel for multi-agency responses among health, police, ambulance and fire services
Requires call centres to have adequate staffing, trained supervisors, mental health supports and direct communication between responders
Mandates a written policy covering communication with callers, accountability for delays, and mandatory reviews after deaths
Amends the Ombudsman Act to create an Assistant Ombudsman overseeing 9-1-1 operations and public awareness campaigns
Enacts the Justice for Soli Act (Stop Criminalizing Mental Health), 2025
Requires the Ontario government to recognize correctional facilities are not appropriate for people in mental health crises
States mental illness requires health care and should not be criminalized
References the inquest into the death of Soleiman (Soli) Faqiri, ruled a homicide
Aligns with the first of 57 recommendations from the Chief Coroner's inquest report
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Declares the week starting on the third Monday of September each year as Consent Awareness Week in Ontario
Aims to promote public understanding and practice of consent
Cites that only 45 per cent of Canadians fully understand what consent entails
References 2019 data showing about 940,000 sexual assault incidents, with only 6 per cent reported to police
Notes 45 colleges and universities already hold Consent Awareness Week activities on campus
Encourages all post-secondary institutions and Ontarians to mark the week with awareness activities
Act takes effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Requires hospitals and long-term care homes in municipalities of 8,000 or more to create plans limiting spending on staffing agencies
Sets timelines to phase out staffing agency use over 24 months, with limits varying by municipality size
Requires new healthcare staffing agencies to operate as not-for-profits
Subjects agencies receiving over $400,000 from government to oversight by Auditor General, Ombudsman, Patient Ombudsman and Integrity Commissioner
Caps agency worker pay at no more than 10 per cent above the existing rate for that profession
Bans agencies from poaching employees from hospitals or long-term care homes, with fines up to $1,000,000
Prohibits agencies from assigning workers to the same or adjacent Ontario Health Team they recently left
Allows the Minister to appoint up to six Deputy Provincial Land and Development Facilitators, up from four
Transfers jurisdiction over highways and bridges from Peel Region to Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon by July 1, 2026 or a date set by the Minister
Transfers jurisdiction over waste collection from Peel Region to Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon by January 1, 2026 or a date set by the Minister
Bars Peel Region from passing a by-law to reclaim waste collection powers from these cities until December 31, 2035
Gives the Minister broad regulation-making power to manage the transfer of assets, staff, contracts and finances between Peel and the three municipalities
Shields the Crown, Peel Region, Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon from lawsuits or damages related to this jurisdiction transfer, even for past actions
Blocks most court, administrative or arbitration claims tied to the transfer, except judicial review or constitutional claims
A large omnibus bill making numerous amendments across 22 different Ontario laws, mostly described as red tape reduction.
Changes range from municipal financial reporting and consumer protection rules to enforcement powers, board compositions, and administrative processes.
Replaces reference to Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade with the responsible Minister.
Allows Ontario Court of Justice to order blood, DNA or other tests in proceedings before it.
Court's jurisdiction to determine parentage is not limited by the Act's parentage rules.
Such a determination is not considered a declaration of parentage under the Act.
Permits disclosure of registry information to a prescribed entity for crime prevention or law enforcement.
Requires an agreement between the Ministry and the entity before such disclosure occurs.
Removes requirement to publish audited financial statements in a newspaper.
City treasurer must instead post the financial information on a City website within 60 days.
Re-enacts rules on rewards points to provide general rules for such consumer agreements.
Allows new regulations governing rewards points agreements.
Regulations may apply retroactively to agreements made before this Act received Royal Assent.
Removes requirement to disclose a person's email address in certain consumer report information.
Expands matters a single Divisional Court judge (instead of a three-judge panel) may decide.
Repeals a provision governing conflicts between Attorney General and Rules Committees on rule-making.
Allows regulations to authorize removal of forest resources without a permit in certain circumstances.
Makes related changes to remedies, compliance orders, liens, and offence provisions.
Updates the definition of 'Minister' in the Act.
Adds a section confirming, for greater certainty, that a specific described agreement is valid and effective.
Re-enacts section requiring Director to publish specified reports, orders and information.
Specifies the minimum time period such publications must remain public.

a.t: Funeral, Burial and Cremation Services Act, 2002
p: Requires operator authorization before providing certain licensed services for human remains.
Allows court applications to determine who has authority over human remains.
Adds new administrative penalties and compliance order enforcement mechanisms.
Changes rules for appointing directors/registrars and handling complaints and inspections.
Requires X-ray owner applicants to provide a current email address and other prescribed information.
Allows service of documents by electronic or other prescribed methods.
Subjects certain Corporation powers to limits imposed under the Ministry of Infrastructure Act, 2011.

a.t: Liquor Control Board of Ontario Act, 2019
p: Subjects certain LCBO powers to limits imposed under the Ministry of Infrastructure Act, 2011.
Permits possession and consumption of open liquor in designated areas of operating provincial parks.
Corrects a French translation inaccuracy regarding 'information under oath'.

a.t: Modernizing Ontario for People and Businesses Act, 2020
p: Authorizes Minister to collect, use and disclose personal information for public consultations on regulatory burdens.
Allows additional vehicle classes to be prescribed as 'motorized snow vehicles'.
Removes requirement to publish municipal financial statements in a newspaper.
Requires posting financial information on municipality's website within 60 days instead.
If no website exists, treasurer must make information available to the public at no cost.

a.t: Ontario Infrastructure and Lands Corporation Act, 2011
p: Adds district social services administration boards as eligible public organizations.
Makes a technical correction to the French version of the Act.

a.t: Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act, 2016
p: Allows Minister to order the Authority to collect and share certain information, kept confidential.
Allows conditions requiring agreements with brand holders for certain product responsibilities.
New provision lets regulations require offering specified services to municipalities.
Changes Board size to no fewer than 13 and no more than 21 trustees.
Reduces number of Lieutenant Governor in Council appointees to between 7 and 15.
Allows electing/appointing body to decide if a replacement trustee serves a full new term.
Allows an attorney or guardian of property to redesignate the same benefit recipient when a plan is converted, renewed, replaced or transferred.
Makes a consequential amendment to a related section.
Amends the Highway Traffic Act to create penalties for offences causing death or serious bodily harm
Applies when a person commits an offence and causes or contributes to an accident causing death or serious injury
Sets a fine of not less than $2,000 and not more than $50,000 on conviction
Allows imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or both fine and imprisonment
Permits suspension of the person's driver's licence or permit for up to five years
Comes into force on the day it receives Royal Assent
Transfers control of Ottawa Road 174 and County Road 17 from a municipality to the Ministry of Transportation
These highways will no longer count as part of any municipality's road system
Existing agreements or permits about the highways continue as if made by the Minister instead
Rights and benefits municipalities had under those agreements now belong to the Crown in right of Ontario
Blocks the Lieutenant Governor in Council from ordering these highways to be transferred back to a municipality
The change takes effect on the day the bill receives Royal Assent
The short title is the Uploading Highways 174 and 17 Act, 2025
Requires scales and inspection sites on Highway 11 north of North Bay and Highway 17 to be staffed at least 12 hours daily
Requires the government to ensure OPP traffic enforcement staffing is sufficient to enforce the Highway Traffic Act
Requires commercial truck drivers to be tested by a Ministry-certified examiner before getting a driver education certificate
Puts the Ministry of Transportation in charge of managing winter maintenance on Highway 11 north of North Bay and Highway 17
Allows the Ministry to work with contractors and providers for winter highway maintenance
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Lets municipalities and local boards charge fees to gas producers, distributors, transmitters and storage companies
Fees can apply for services, activities, costs payable or use of property on municipal highways
Applies to wires, cables, poles, conduits, pipes, equipment, machinery or other works used in the gas business
Blocks provincial regulations from limiting this municipal fee-charging power
Makes matching changes to both the Municipal Act, 2001 and the City of Toronto Act, 2006
Comes into force immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Short title is the No Free Ride for Fossil Fuels Act, 2025
Requires landlords to keep rental properties in good repair regardless of any effort made to do so
Lets tenants apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board when a landlord ignores a mediated settlement or prior repair order
Allows fines up to $1,000 per day or rent abatements for landlords who fail to complete ordered repairs
Sets new rules capping rent charged to a new tenant based on the previous tenant's lawful rent
Creates a public rent registry requiring landlords to file rent and address information within 30 days of a new lease
Bars landlords from raising rent if they have not filed the required registry statement
Requires free mandatory legal representation for tenants facing above-guideline rent increase applications
Amends the Building Code Act, 1992 to require new houses to be built EV-charger ready
Applies to new houses under Part 9 of the building code with a garage, carport or driveway
Requires builders to install a minimum 200 amp panel board in these homes
Requires a conduit of at least 27 mm trade size with a means to pull cables through
Requires a square 4-11/16 inch electrical outlet box near the garage, carport or driveway
Conduit and outlet box must block gas and exhaust fumes from passing through
Rules apply only to houses built after the section comes into force
Requires new or renovated correctional institutions to have at least 20 percent of inmate beds in mental health support units
Prohibits cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment or punishment of inmates
Bans overly rigorous physical restraints, excessive surveillance, sensory deprivation and disorientation of inmates
Prohibits withholding food, exercise, human contact or medical care as punishment
Requires superintendents to ensure treatment complies with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Bans segregation, defined as highly restricted movement and association for 22 or more hours a day
Creates an Independent Review Panel to review cases of inmates held in restrictive confinement
Reverses 2015 changes to the Government Advertising Act, restoring earlier Auditor General review rules
Bans government offices from publishing, displaying or broadcasting ads before Auditor General review results are received
Requires ads to state they are paid for by the Government of Ontario
Bans use of Executive Council or Assembly members' names, voices or images in government ads, with exceptions for ads targeted outside Ontario
Bans partisan advertising or ads primarily meant to boost the governing party's image or attack critics
Restricts government ads during election writ periods, with exceptions for revenue-generating or time-sensitive items
Renames the law the End the Public Funding of Partisan Government Advertising Act, 2025
Requires the Ontario government to formally recognize intimate partner violence as an epidemic in the province
Directs the Attorney General to create a Renfrew County Inquest Implementation Committee within 30 days of the section taking effect
Committee membership must equally split between senior ministry officials and community experts on intimate partner violence
One community expert member must chair the Committee
Committee will review the 86 recommendations from the 2022 Renfrew County triple femicide inquest and plan implementation steps
Committee must publish a first report within 12 months, then updates every 12 months, tabled in the Legislature and posted online
Lieutenant Governor in Council may set remuneration and expenses for members, subject to funds being appropriated by the Legislature
Bill 56 is an omnibus bill amending 11 different Ontario laws covering water protection, forestry, health professions, highway traffic, heritage, labour mobility and species conservation.
Many changes aim to streamline approvals, update regulatory references, and adjust rules for health profession registration, source water protection and speed enforcement.
Restricts source protection plan policies for activities identified as significant drinking water threats, per Minister's rules.
Requires Minister to publish notice on environmental registry after plan amendments are deemed approved.
Adds deemed approval of amendments if Minister doesn't act within 120 days or prescribed period.
New section requires certain decisions to conform to specific source protection plan policies.
Allows one forest management plan to cover multiple forest management units.
Repeals requirement for annual Minister approval before licence holders can harvest.
Extends Minister's stop-work and penalty powers to licence holders as well as permittees.
Shifts power to approve and amend manuals from Cabinet to the Minister.
Expands definitions referring to pharmacists to include additional prescribed persons.
Allows certain actions under the Act to apply to these prescribed persons.
Adds a related regulation-making power and other minor amendments.
Removes specific references to prescribed persons in two clauses and adds a general power to prescribe persons instead.
Lets the Minister direct municipalities to install school zone signs, and install them if municipality fails to.
Repeals the part of the Act authorizing automated speed enforcement systems.
Extinguishes certain causes of action related to this repeal and makes consequential amendments.
Replaces reference to the Agreement on Internal Trade with the Canadian Free Trade Agreement.
Corrects English wording from 'investigation' to 'inspection' to match related provision.
Adds rules for individuals deemed certified in a regulated occupation.
Adds a corresponding regulation-making power and makes technical amendments.
Allows prescribed persons to perform specified acts in audiology, dental technology, dentistry and denturism.
Creates a faster registration procedure for out-of-province applicants with limited requirements allowed.
Lets Registrars impose interim suspensions on out-of-province members pending Registration Committee review.
Replaces references to the Agreement on Internal Trade with the Canadian Free Trade Agreement.
Clarifies the Act's purpose is to protect species at risk.
Expands definition of 'section 16 activity' to include parts of listed species, living or dead.
Addresses species previously listed as extirpated, endangered or threatened under the old Endangered Species Act, 2007.
Repeals and replaces subsection 37(1) to align with section 38, plus other technical changes.

a.t: Amendments to Regulated Health Profession Statutes
p: Adds power to make regulations exempting prescribed persons from title protection rules across several health profession Acts.

a.t: Consequential Amendments in Respect of the Species Conservation Act, 2025 and Other Related Amendments
p: Exempts certain forest operations from Species Conservation Act prohibitions and related orders.
Updates references across several Acts from the old Species at Risk list to the new Protected Species in Ontario List.
Adds a 'species at risk' definition tied to Committee on the Status of Species at Risk in Ontario classifications in park-related Acts.
Adds the Species Conservation Act, 2025 to the definition of 'prescribed instrument' under the Lake Simcoe Protection Act, 2008.
Vacates the seat of the Haldimand County trustee on the Brant Haldimand Norfolk Catholic District School Board
The trustee traveled to Europe with three others in July 2024 using Board-reimbursed public funds
This trustee refused to repay $12,370 in expenses, unlike three colleagues who repaid in full
Bars this trustee from running for any school board office in the next regular election
Bans this trustee from being appointed or running in any school board by-election until November 14, 2030
Blocks lawsuits or claims for damages against the Crown, the school board, or Haldimand County over this law
Allows only judicial review or constitutional remedy claims, not other compensation claims
Creates the Franco-Ontarian Bookstore Promotion and Protection Act, 2025
Requires the Minister of Francophone Affairs to appoint a Registrar to accredit Franco-Ontarian bookstores
Bookstores can apply for accreditation if they sell French-language books and support Franco-Ontarian culture
Publicly funded institutions must buy French-language books only from accredited Franco-Ontarian bookstores, starting six months after Royal Assent
Bans predatory pricing and hidden discounts aimed at unfairly capturing institutional book sales
Allows revocation of a bookstore's accreditation if it breaks these pricing rules
Lets the Minister create a funded support program for bookstore modernization and lets government agencies be required to support Franco-Ontarian cultural institutions
Requires Ontario to implement recommendations from the 2017 Rare Diseases Working Group Report as soon as practicable
Notes these recommendations were never implemented since the 2017 report
Requires government to post a public update every six months on progress
Updates must list which recommendations are done and steps for remaining ones
Updates continue every six months until all recommendations are implemented
Amends the Health Protection and Promotion Act to add this requirement
Short title is the Rare Disease Strategy Act, 2025

Amends 15 existing Ontario Acts and creates a new one, mainly to speed up transit, housing and infrastructure projects and to adjust rules on development charges, tenancies, driver's licences and water/sewage services.
Expands ministerial and municipal powers over construction, transit corridors, water infrastructure and land use, while shortening some notice periods and review timelines.
Removes definition of 'immediate danger to construction', folding it into section 26.
Expands construction references to include operation and maintenance in several sections.
Reduces notice periods from 30 days to 15 days in sections 14, 17, 19 and 36.
Broadens Metrolinx's power over municipal service/right of way access, including bridges and life safety systems.
Re-enacts section 30 to cover abandonment or termination of contracts, not just default.
Repeals not-yet-in-force amendments to section 31, keeping only notice-of-termination provisions.
Adds transition rule for project agreements and adjusts transition rules for section 31 changes.
Transfers transitional regulation-making power from Lieutenant Governor in Council to the Minister.
Requires a separate development charge class for certain capital costs, with exceptions.
Requires councils to give background studies and by-laws to the Minister on request by set deadlines.
Moves treasurer's financial statement deadline to June 30, copy to Minister by July 15.
Requires municipalities to create and regularly review local service policies for development charges.
Allows a transit station charge to be collected for residential developments, with related new provisions.
Lets the Minister require proof of Ontario residency, legal status and work ability for certain licences.
Restricts municipalities from reducing traffic lane numbers in certain situations.
Changes reimbursement rules for municipalities handling bicycle lane removal or reconfiguration.
Allows owners of prescribed tax-exempt land to voluntarily pay a Minister-approved amount for local road work.
Adds related record-keeping and payment submission requirements.
Transfers water and sewage utility jurisdiction from Peel Region to Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon within their areas.
Expands when section 53 applies to multiple sewage works on one agricultural property based on design capacity thresholds.
Lets the Minister require proof of Ontario residency and legal status in Canada from photo card applicants.
Ministerial decisions no longer need to match provincial policy statements, except for Greenbelt Area land.
Removes upper-tier municipalities' general power to designate community improvement project areas, replacing with new rule.
Allows municipalities to reduce minimum or increase maximum standards in zoning by-laws under new rules.
Lets Minister-required development agreements be delegated to municipal officers, with new timeline and enforcement powers.

a.t: Public Transportation and Highway Improvement Act
p: States certain actions under the Act never constituted expropriation or injurious affection.
Replaces section 117 to let the Minister exempt specified highways/bridges from standard planning and construction rules.
Authorizes regulations on contracts and required reporting for highway and bridge work.
Standardizes notice forms as Board-approved unless a form is prescribed.
Lets regulations define 'persistent failure to pay rent' for eviction purposes.
Requires tenants to pay half of claimed arrears among new conditions to set aside eviction orders.
Sets a 15-day deadline to request review of Board decisions, unless extended for fairness.
Adjusts timelines and procedures for winding up the Corporation; removes an expired reporting requirement.

a.t: Towing and Storage Safety and Enforcement Act, 2021
p: Removes requirement to submit charge amounts to the Director if a regulation sets a maximum chargeable amount.
Allows the Minister to establish an advisory panel with defined functions and composition.
Lets the Minister require landowners to sign development agreements with municipalities.
Requires municipalities to designate a person to report information on transit-oriented community land to the Minister.

a.t: Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025
p: Enacts new Act letting the Minister designate corporations to provide water/sewage services for certain municipalities.
Gives these corporations power to collect fees and charges for services.
Lets the Minister set rules on corporate boards, share issuance, and required rate plans.
Extinguishes certain causes of action related to the Act.
Requires Ontario to create a 10-year strategy to become a global leader in artificial intelligence and innovation
Sets 12 objectives, including boosting AI startups, research funding, talent retention, and protecting privacy and safety
Creates an Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee of up to 21 members within 90 days of the Act taking effect
Committee must include representatives from AI industry, labour, health care, Indigenous groups, disability rights, and other sectors
Committee must publish an initial report within 180 days and an annual progress report thereafter
Minister must respond publicly to Committee recommendations within 90 days and table reports in the Legislature within 60 days
Requires a legislative committee to review the Act's effectiveness every three years
Makes the Chief Medical Officer of Health an independent officer of the Legislative Assembly
Requires the Assembly to appoint the Chief Medical Officer through an all-party selection panel
Sets a five-year term, renewable once, for the Chief Medical Officer of Health
Allows removal only by a two-thirds vote of the Assembly, or suspension for cause in specific cases
Creates a process to appoint a temporary Chief Medical Officer if the position is vacant or the officer cannot serve
Requires a select committee to advise and receive advice from the Chief Medical Officer during declared public health emergencies
Sets pay, pension and expense rules for the Chief Medical Officer, decided by the Board of Internal Economy
Amends the Ticket Sales Act, 2017 to cap resale ticket prices
Bans reselling tickets on the secondary market for more than 50 per cent above face value
Price cap includes fees and service charges but excludes applicable taxes
Applies to anyone selling or facilitating the sale of tickets above the new limit
Law takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Stop Ripping Off Fans Act (Ticket Resale Price Caps), 2025
Requires landlords to keep common areas at 26 degrees Celsius or less from May 15 to September 15, with municipal inspection and work orders
Requires digital visitor parking registration systems in buildings with 100 or more rental units and bans charging fees for visitor parking
Sets a 20 percent rent abatement if a vital service is withheld for more than 24 hours over three months
Requires video surveillance systems and a security guard in buildings with 100 or more rental units
Gives a 5 percent rent abatement if an elevator is out of service for more than 48 hours over three months
Requires landlords to publish yearly maintenance statistics online, limiting rent increases if less than 90 percent of requests are resolved
Requires elevator owners to use remote monitoring and report outages longer than 24 hours to the Technical Standards and Safety Authority
Requires every school to hold a dedicated Remembrance Day service on November 11, or the preceding Friday if it falls on a weekend
Allows services to include cenotaph visits, wreath laying, assemblies, musical tributes, or similar commemorations
Bans services made up entirely of prerecorded material
Directs the Ministry of Education to create elementary and secondary curricula on the purpose and importance of Remembrance Day
Requires the curriculum to cover both historical and modern military conflicts
Requires consultation with educators and their unions when developing the curriculum
Prohibits workplaces from operating between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. on Remembrance Day, unless exempted by regulation
Declares October each year as Kids' Online Safety and Privacy Month in Ontario
Aims to raise awareness about children's safety and privacy online
Highlights risks like cyberbullying, online grooming, exploitation and trafficking
Emphasizes role of parents, educators and community in supervising children's internet use
Short title given is the Kids' Online Safety and Privacy Month Act, 2025
Act took effect on the day it received Royal Assent
Declares February 23 each year as Hospitality Workers Appreciation Day in Ontario
Aims to recognize contributions of restaurant, hotel, event venue and catering workers
Short title is the Hospitality Workers Appreciation Day Act, 2025
Act took effect on the day it received Royal Assent

This budget-implementation omnibus bill amends 18 different Ontario laws, covering climate targets, health agencies, conservation authorities, elections, pensions, insurance, taxes and provincial spending authority.
It removes climate reporting requirements, restructures conservation authority oversight, changes election timing rules, adjusts tax credits, and authorizes government spending for 2026-2027.
Repeals sections requiring government to set greenhouse gas reduction targets and prepare climate change plans and reports.
Certain Ontario Health assets and revenues no longer form part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
All Ontario Health atHome assets and revenues excluded from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Removes Lieutenant Governor in Council approval for borrowing, lending or investing; replaced with ministerial by-law approval.
Related financing must generally be arranged through the Ontario Financing Authority.
Establishes the Ontario Provincial Conservation Agency to oversee conservation authorities and a new regional watershed framework.
Minister may direct the Agency; the Agency may direct conservation authorities after notifying the Minister.
Agency can set and collect fees and recover costs and expenses.
Adds liability protections for specified persons and new regulation-making powers.
Requires corporations under section 140.2 of the Business Corporations Act to file returns on individuals with significant control.
Minister may share this information with specified persons and regulatory bodies.

a.t: Credit Unions and Caisses Populaires Act, 2020
p: Allows sale of credit union securities to non-members in certain circumstances.
Adjusts voting rights and director-election rights for non-members.
Changes how instalment payments for school tax remittances are calculated under section 257.11.
Municipalities must provide information returns to the Minister of Finance on request regarding instalments and payments in lieu of taxes.
A consequential amendment is made to the Assessment Act.
Repeals the fixed four-year election cycle held on the first Thursday in June.
Changes timing of targeted voter registration programs.
Removes pre-election fiscal review requirement and pre-election advertising publication ban.
Adds a rule that no Legislative Assembly may continue longer than five years.
Chief Electoral Officer gains power to investigate third parties and demand information from them.
Raises contribution limits to registered parties and indexes future limits to inflation.
Continues quarterly allowances to registered parties and constituency associations.
Requires proof of registration before third-party political ads may run, with broadcaster/publisher compliance duties and expanded penalty provisions.
Sets new filing deadline for employers ceasing an Ontario permanent establishment due to an amalgamation: earlier of six months after amalgamation or March 15 of following year.

a.t: Fiscal Sustainability, Transparency and Accountability Act, 2019
p: Replaces references to 'provincial net debt' with 'provincial net financial liabilities' throughout the Act.
Allows reassessment of health system costs under section 14.1.
Transitional Authority rules prevail over conflicting Act or regulation provisions.
Insurers must reimburse all pharmacy operators equally for a given dispensed drug, subject to limits.
Allows designation of public sector reciprocal insurance exchanges, with supervisor appointment powers and new regulation-making authority.
Authorizes government expenditures up to set maximum amounts pending supply votes for the 2026-2027 fiscal year.

a.t: Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System Act, 2006
p: Minister may order the Sponsors Corporation to wind up, with detailed winding-up rules.
Replaces the Sponsors Corporation with a new Sponsors Council with defined objects and composition.
Minister may appoint the Administration Corporation's Chair for a term starting April 15, 2026, up to three years.
Adds liability protections and bars certain legal proceedings against Crown and corporation officials.
Sets rules for converting single-employer defined contribution plans into jointly sponsored pension plans, with member opt-out rights.
Adds similar conversion rules for plans with both defined benefit and defined contribution components.
Expands successor pension plan rules to include jointly sponsored pension plans.
Allows transfer of defined contribution assets when an employer joins a jointly sponsored pension plan.
Fixes land identified by Property Identification Number as of the day it is added, unaffected by later PIN changes.
Allows regulations to limit the extent or duration of land vesting.
Broadens regulation-making power to cover the whole Ontario Place Redevelopment Project, not just construction.
Removes requirement for Toronto and the Corporation to promptly negotiate municipal service and right-of-way terms.
Authorizes additional expenditures, beyond the 2024 interim appropriation, pending supply votes for the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
Creates a new expanded Ontario made manufacturing investment tax credit for eligible expenditures between May 15, 2025 and January 1, 2030.
Adds an extra 5% credit rate for eligible property available for use in that same window under the existing manufacturing tax credit.
Creates a new Ontario shortline railway investment tax credit requiring certification by the Minister of Transportation.
Retroactively adjusts small beer manufacturers' tax credit formulas, Trillium Benefit/child benefit indexation, and property tax credit rules for land lease and specified homes.
Removes certain lands from provincial park status under the Provincial Parks and Conservation Reserves Act, 2006.
Designates some of those lands as a historical park under the Historical Parks Act.
