Requires the Minister to ensure 70 per cent of staff at larger hospitals, long-term care homes, home care agencies or health providers are permanent full-time employees
This 70 per cent rule applies only where the employer has more than 20 individuals employed
Personal support workers must be paid at least $8.00 more than minimum wage for each hour worked
Full-time personal support workers get at least 10 paid sick/illness leave days per year, part-time pro-rated
Personal support workers must receive health benefits and pension plan membership
Homemakers must be paid at least minimum wage and get standard hours, eating period and overtime rules under the Employment Standards Act
The Act takes effect one year after receiving Royal Assent
Requires Metrolinx to promote integration of routes, fares and schedules of municipal bike share systems
Requires at least 20 per cent of residential units on sold or disposed Metrolinx assets to be affordable units
Sets mandatory maintenance standards for Highways 11, 17 and 69
Requires snow removal from highway pavement within four hours after a snowfall ends
Requires ice on the pavement to be cleared within three hours of being noticed
Requires potholes over 600 square centimetres and eight centimetres deep to be repaired within four days

Requires the Minister to develop a public plan within 12 months to convert these highways to a 2+1 lane configuration, with construction starting one year after publication and finishing within five years, plus annual progress reports
Creates the Life Leases Act, 2025, setting up rules for life lease housing agreements in Ontario
Defines a life lease as an agreement letting someone occupy a residential unit for life or a fixed minimum term
Overrides conflicting agreements or waivers and voids lease terms inconsistent with the Act
Bans life lease sponsors from knowingly giving false or misleading information
Sets fines up to $50,000 for individuals and $250,000 for corporations for offences under the Act
Allows directors or officers to be held liable if they knowingly participate in an offence
Gives government power to make regulations on financial disclosures, reserve funds, meetings and lease terms, even for existing leases
Creates a new law letting the government require public sector bodies to favour Ontario or Canadian made goods and services in their purchasing, and repeals the previous 'Buy Ontario' law.
Also lets the Minister of Transportation order municipalities to install community safety zone signs, and protects certain condominium law provisions from automatic repeal.
Lets Management Board of Cabinet issue directives requiring public sector entities to follow procurement rules.
Directives can require preference for Ontario or Canadian made goods or services.
Requires third-party supply chain managers to comply via contract with public sector entities.
Allows withholding funds from non-compliant organizations and repeals the Building Ontario Businesses Initiative Act, 2022.
Minister may direct a municipality to install signs in community safety zones.
If municipality fails to install signs, the Minister may install them instead.
New regulation-making power to require flashing amber signals in school and community safety zones.
Amends automatic repeal process for long-unproclaimed Acts.
Certain provisions of the Protecting Condominium Owners Act, 2015 are exempted from repeal on December 31, 2025.
Creates the Protecting Ontario from Urban Wildfires Act, 2025, requiring an Urban Wildfires Advisory Committee within 90 days
Committee includes climate and wildfire scientists, firefighters, conservation authorities, municipalities and First Nations representatives
Committee must assess growing urban wildfire risks and timelines, and recommend prevention and response measures
Committee must report its findings and recommendations to the Legislative Assembly within one year of being formed
Minister must develop plans and any needed legislation within a year of that report to address urban wildfires
Plans may update Building Code, zoning rules, and laws like the Emergency Management and Forest Fires Prevention Acts
Minister must also create education programs for city residents and protocols for cooperation between urban and forest firefighting forces
Amends Christopher's Law to expand who can access sex offender registry information
Allows disclosure of registry information to prescribed entities for crime prevention or law enforcement purposes
Requires the Ministry to enter into an agreement with a prescribed entity before disclosing information to it
Permits prescribed entities to collect, retain and use disclosed information for crime prevention or law enforcement purposes
Gives government power to make regulations naming prescribed entities and governing these agreements
Keeps existing disclosure rules for police services and policing entities from other jurisdictions

Amends seven Ontario laws covering animal research and welfare, bail enforcement, coroners' inquests, dangerous driving penalties, police record checks, and a scholarship fund for fallen public safety officers' families.
Overall aims include tightening bail lien collection, increasing penalties for dangerous drivers and animal harm, and adding new protections and procedures across justice and animal welfare systems.
Prohibits invasive medical research on cats, dogs and other prescribed animals, with specific exceptions.
Other research on these animals is banned unless specific conditions are met.
Sets out animal care committee roles and bans breeding cats/dogs for research at supply facilities.
Establishes minor and major offences with maximum penalties, plus technical registration changes.
Certificates of lien are now registered against land in the land registry office, not sent to the sheriff.
Crown may enforce unpaid surety debts by selling the registered property.
Liens expire six years after registration unless specified conditions apply.
New rules let the Crown require payment from an accused or surety for breached release conditions.

a.t: Constable Joe MacDonald Public Safety Officers’ Survivors Scholarship Fund Act, 2026
p: Continues the existing scholarship fund for surviving spouses and children of public safety officers killed on duty.
Sets rules for granting scholarships, including circumstances to be prescribed by regulation.
Continues the Fund's governing Committee and sets rules for its membership and functions.
Adds new regulation-making powers respecting the Fund and its scholarships.
Replaces pathologist instruction duties with new requirements for postgraduate training and continuing education.
Bans photographs, audio/video recordings or other records at inquests and related contexts.
Prohibits publishing or reproducing such records, with limited exceptions for notes, sketches or authorized recordings.
Makes violations of these recording rules an offence.
Allows indefinite licence suspension for a Criminal Code conviction of dangerous driving causing death.
Lets police suspend a licence and impound a vehicle on suspected dangerous driving offences.
Creates a right to appeal vehicle impoundment for driving while suspended.
Increases fines and suspension periods for driving while suspended and for phone/screen use by commercial drivers.
Clarifies that summary-conviction-only offences are excluded from disclosure if requested more than five years after conviction.
Requires police record check providers to follow prescribed service standards.
Extinguishes certain legal claims related to failures to meet those service standards.
Gives the Minister power to make regulations setting and enforcing these service standards.
Raises the minimum fine for harming an animal that works with peace officers to $50,000.
Sets a flat maximum fine of $260,000 for individuals and $1,000,000 for corporations, regardless of repeat offences.
Makes consequential amendments to reflect these changed penalties.
Corrects errors in the French version of the Act.
Annexes parts of Oro-Medonte and Springwater townships into the City of Barrie, effective January 1, 2026 or Royal Assent, whichever is later.
Transfers real property like roads, waterlines and sewers in the annexed areas to Barrie, while other assets and liabilities stay with the original municipalities.
Keeps existing by-laws, official plans and in-progress municipal procedures in force until Barrie changes them.
Requires unpaid property taxes in annexed areas to be paid to Barrie, with special tax rolls and repayments to the townships.
Phases in higher property tax rates for annexed properties over 2026-2030, or 2026-2045 for farm and managed forest properties.
Allows the Minister to set regulations on ward boundaries, compensation payments between municipalities, and other transition details.
Protects council members of Oro-Medonte and Springwater from disqualification due solely to the annexation until November 14, 2026.
Amends the Occupational Health and Safety Act to strengthen protections against workplace reprisals
Requires hospitals and long-term care homes to publicly post monthly counts of workplace violence incidents on their websites
Requires hospitals and long-term care homes to publicly post monthly counts of workplace harassment incidents on their websites
Prohibits reprisals against workers who report, speak out publicly, or testify about workplace violence or harassment
Defines a reprisal as any measure that adversely affects a worker's employment, such as firing, demotion, discipline or intimidation
Protects workers who participate in violence or harassment investigations or give information to health and safety committees or inspectors
Takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Creates a new independent officer of the Legislature called the Commissioner for Democratic Rights
Commissioner appointed by unanimous agreement of an all-party panel chaired by the Speaker, unless the Assembly agrees otherwise
Commissioner serves a five-year term, renewable once for another five years
Commissioner can appoint a Deputy Commissioner and other staff as needed
Commissioner monitors barriers to voting and reviews laws and government actions affecting democratic rights
Commissioner reviews provincial interference in local governments and councils, and promotes civic education
Commissioner can question people under oath, hold public inquiries and conduct investigations
Bans passing another vehicle by crossing double solid yellow lines on a highway
Applies to vehicles going in the same direction as the one being passed
Sets a $400 fine for breaking this rule
Adds three or more demerit points for the offence
Amends the Highway Traffic Act's Section 148
Known as Chad's Law (Enforcing Safer Passing), 2025
Creates the Gender Affirming Health Care Advisory Committee Act, 2025
Minister of Health must establish an Advisory Committee within 60 days of the Act coming into force
Committee members appointed by the Minister, aiming for a majority from transgender, two-spirit, non-binary, intersex and gender diverse communities
Committee must reflect diversity including youth, seniors, Indigenous persons, racialized groups, and people with disabilities
Committee will recommend ways to improve access, coverage, and reduce wait times for gender affirming health care
Committee must consult groups like Rainbow Health Ontario and health care providers, then report within six months
Minister must tell the Legislature which recommendations the government will implement within 90 days of the report
Creates a Strategic Action Plan, due within two years, to protect Ontarians from climate change risks like floods, heat, storms and wildfires
Establishes an arm's-length Ontario Climate Adaptation Fund to finance adaptation and resilience projects
Sets up an Ontario Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience Resource Centre for climate data, research and public advice
Creates a Whole-of-Government Climate Adaptation Co-ordination Secretariat to align policy across all ministries and agencies
Requires the Legislature to review the strategic action plan every two years starting four years after enactment
Mandates specific measures on flood mapping, extreme heat cooling, wildfire response, infrastructure codes and farmland protection
Proposes an Ontario Youth Climate Corps offering wages and education support for climate-related work
Landlords seeking above guideline rent increases for capital expenditures must submit engineering reports and cost evidence
New exceptions block increases for cosmetic upgrades, routine maintenance, or landlord-caused repairs
Board must consider tenant's rent burden, local vacancy rates, and housing options before approving increases
Board can dismiss applications if the increase would cause undue hardship for tenants
Costs from non-arm's-length deals or government-funded work cannot count toward rent increase calculations
Replaces 'serious breach' standard with lower 'breach' threshold for landlord obligation violations
Landlords must give 30 days notice before reducing rent after a capital expenditure increase ends, or pay tenants 1.5 times any overpayment
Proclaims December of each year as Christian Heritage Month in Ontario
States purpose is to reflect on and celebrate historical roots and contributions of Ontario's Christian community
Preamble notes Christian pioneers' role in shaping Ontario's cultural, social and artistic development since before Confederation
Preamble highlights diversity of Ontario's Christian community including Latin American, European, First Nations, African, Asian and Middle Eastern heritage
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Christian Heritage Month Act, 2025
Amends the Mandatory Blood Testing Act, 2006 to address cases involving deceased persons
If a respondent dies after an application is made, the process continues with modifications set by regulations
Allows a person to apply for blood testing of someone who is already deceased at the time of application
Deceased-person applications will be handled entirely under rules set out in regulations, not the usual sections 3 to 6
Minister gains power to make regulations covering hearings, Board decisions and court orders for these new situations
Updates references in sections 7 and 8 to apply more broadly to orders made under the Act
Act takes effect on a date to be set later by the Lieutenant Governor in Council
Creates the Transparent and Accountable Health Care Act, 2025 for Ontario health funding oversight
Defines major health sector organizations as those receiving at least $1 million yearly from the Ministry of Health starting fiscal 2027
Defines publicly-funded suppliers as those receiving at least $1 million yearly, directly or indirectly, from those organizations or other suppliers
Requires these organizations and suppliers to follow the Broader Public Sector Executive Compensation Act, 2014
Requires them to disclose salaries under the Public Sector Salary Disclosure Act, 1996
Makes them subject to complaints under the Ombudsman Act as governmental organizations
Lets the Auditor General audit any aspect of their operations in qualifying fiscal years
Replaces the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997 with the new Meredith Act (Fair Compensation for Injured Workers), 2025
Sets lost-earnings compensation at 90 per cent of a worker's deemed income, indexed to inflation each year
Creates the Workers' Compensation Commission of Ontario to administer benefits and collect employer premiums
Establishes the Workers' Compensation Appeals Tribunal of Ontario to hear disputes over Commission decisions
Requires the Commission to cover medically appropriate treatment, medication, devices, education and retraining for injured workers
Protects injured workers' jobs, requiring employers to accommodate them up to undue hardship
Sets a six-year transition period to review and reassess all workers currently receiving benefits under the old Act
Amends the Environmental Protection Act to require a Minister's review of Ontario Regulation 103/94 rules
Regulation 103/94 covers industrial, commercial and institutional source separation programs
Review must start no more than three months after the section takes effect
Goal is to set clear, enforceable outcomes-based requirements like diversion targets, disposal caps or contamination thresholds
Minister must consider factors like sector scope, facility size thresholds, designated materials, reporting, audits and multi-residential diversion methods
Minister must report findings to the Legislative Assembly within nine months of starting the review
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Requires the Registrar to create a trauma-informed sexual violence and harassment prevention training program for licensed premises
Servers, security staff and their supervisors must complete this training before starting their duties
Licence and permit holders must display a sign showing staff completed the training
Existing licensees and workers get four months after the law takes effect to complete training
Every licensee and permit holder must have a written sexual violence and harassment policy with community support information
Expands the Occupational Health and Safety Act definition of workplace violence to include workplace sexual violence
Requires employers and all workers to complete Chief Prevention Officer-approved training on workplace sexual harassment
Creates the Massage Therapy Tax Act, 2025 in Ontario
Requires the Minister of Health to make tax treatment of massage therapy services consistent
Aims to equalize taxes whether services are provided by registered massage therapists or other practitioners
Allows the Minister to introduce further legislation if needed to achieve this equal tax treatment
Cites regulated massage therapy's role in pain management, injury rehab and well-being as background
Comes into force immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Amends the Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act, 2016 to address textile waste
Minister must start a review within three months to include textiles as a designated waste material
Minister must consult clothing companies, waste service providers, non-profits, municipalities and the Resource Productivity and Recovery Authority
Responsibility for textile waste should generally fall on the brand holder, importer or retailer based in Canada
Minister must report findings and a timeline to the Legislative Assembly within six months of starting the review
A progress update is required three months after that report
If textiles remain undesignated, the Minister must report every two months until they are designated
Creates a right to repair for electronics, appliances, farm equipment, vehicles, mobility aids and recreational vehicles
Requires suppliers to give consumers or repair shops manuals, parts, tools and software needed for repairs
Suppliers must generally provide documentation free and can only charge reasonable fees for parts, tools and software
Suppliers must keep repair information for at least 7 years and vehicle repair data for at least 10 years
Bans parts pairing tricks that block, weaken or overcharge for independent repairs
Lets consumers get a free replacement or refund if a supplier refuses or cannot provide required repair support
Allows courts to declare seriously defective motor vehicles and order repurchase, replacement or lease termination
Creates the Ontario Consumer Watchdog Act, 2025 to protect consumers
Requires the Minister to develop a plan for an independent consumer watchdog organization
Plan must be created with input from stakeholders and the public
Watchdog would investigate businesses, handle complaints, and impose penalties for violations
Organization could establish education and policy research centres for consumer protection
Minister must publish the plan online and table a progress report within six months
Watchdog's decisions could override other regulatory bodies in specified sectors
Requires regular inspections of driving schools offering truck driver Class A training programs
Schools licensed under five years must be inspected at least every six months
Schools licensed five or more years must be inspected at least once every calendar year
Inspections must be done jointly with inspectors appointed under the Highway Traffic Act
Inspectors must prepare a joint inspection report within two weeks of the inspection
Minister must publish inspection results on a government website within 30 days of receiving the report
Short title is the Truck Driver Training Schools Accountability Act, 2026
Amends the Ticket Sales Act, 2017 to ban reselling tickets above face value
Prohibits offering or facilitating secondary market ticket sales above face value
Price cap includes fees and service charges but excludes applicable taxes
Removes a related clause about total amounts exceeding face value from existing law
Takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Putting Fans First Act (No Ticket Resales Above Face Value), 2026
Authorizes up to $213,952,841,200 in public service expenses for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026
Authorizes up to $8,421,348,400 for public service investments in capital assets, loans and other investments
Authorizes up to $406,088,900 for expenses of Legislative Offices like Auditor General and Ombudsman
Health receives the largest ministry allocation, over $80.3 billion in Schedule A
Education is allocated about $40.9 billion, the second largest ministry total
Repeals the Interim Appropriation for 2025-2026 Act, 2024 and its supplementary version
This Act itself is deemed repealed starting April 1, 2027
Bans employers from using replacement workers to do the jobs of striking or locked-out employees
Prohibits using bargaining unit employees, newly hired staff, or transferred employees to perform struck work
Allows replacement workers only for specific emergency services like custody, residential care, or ambulance services
Requires employers to notify the union before using replacement workers for permitted emergency services
Lets unions consent to use their own members instead of replacement workers for that emergency work
Guarantees striking or locked-out employees the right to their old job back after the dispute ends
Requires employers to accept union payments to keep employee benefits like insurance active during a strike or lock-out
A wide-ranging budget bill covering city by-laws, conservation authority mergers, taxes, borrowing, pensions, freedom of information, ticket resale rules and workplace safety board appointments.
It creates new bodies and funds, sets tax rates and credits, and adjusts rules on holidays, privacy requests and pension benefits.
Enacts a new Act exempting block 18C from a Toronto by-law provision (section 10(4)).
Repeals the Skydome Act (Bus Parking), 2002.
Limits by-laws on business closings so they cannot apply to Family Day or Victoria Day.
Amalgamates 35 conservation authorities into 8 new ones and renames Lakehead as Northwestern Ontario Regional Conservation Authority.
First members appointed by participating municipalities; transition committees set up by the Ontario Provincial Conservation Agency.
During transition, creating, enlarging, amalgamating or dissolving authorities is prohibited; Minister may issue directions.
Requires each authority to establish watershed councils to identify local priorities and interests.
Changes rules letting funded benefit plans elect to be taxed as unfunded benefit plans.
Minister may make regulations, possibly retroactive, on tax payable when elections are made or revoked.
Revokes a related regulation.
Creates the Protect Ontario Account Investment Fund for investments in innovation, infrastructure and economic growth.
Minister of Finance may direct investment proceeds to stay in the Consolidated Revenue Fund instead.
Repeals current requirements for transactions increasing Ontario's debt or contingent liabilities, with some transition rules.
Revokes related exception regulations and makes consequential amendments to other Acts.

a.t: Fiscal Sustainability, Transparency and Accountability Act, 2019
p: Changes the requirement for including a progress update on the debt burden reduction strategy in the annual budget.

a.t: Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act
p: Switches certain time limits to be calculated in business days.
Allows staged access plans for records requests and an extra time-limit extension in some cases.
Permits disclosure of personal info to let transferred or assigned employees keep online account access.
Removes mandatory reviews of data integration units and changes how data standards are set.
Excludes people registered as Indians under the Indian Act (Canada) from the definition of 'foreign national'.
Makes various changes to tax rates on beer, wine, wine cooler and spirits.
Limits by-laws on retail business closings so they cannot apply to Family Day or Victoria Day.

a.t: Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act
p: Switches certain time limits to be calculated in business days.
Allows staged access plans and an extra time-limit extension for responding to requests.
Adds privacy impact assessment duties and reporting of data breaches to the Commissioner.
Excludes certain records under the Enhancing Digital Security and Trust Act, 2024 from the Act.
Authorizes the Crown to borrow up to $35 billion.
Creates 'variable life benefits' paid from a new variable life benefit fund within a pension fund.
Sets rules for transferring amounts into such funds, death benefits, and partial wind ups.
For wind ups on or after March 26, 2026, amounts of pension over $3,000 are not guaranteed by the Pension Benefits Guarantee Fund.
New process lets administrators apply to extinguish benefits of untraceable people over 100 years old.
Removes Victoria Day from the definition of 'holiday' under the Act.
Sets the Ontario dividend tax credit at 15.2283 per cent for years after December 31, 2026.
Sets the small business deduction rate at 9.3 per cent for days after June 30, 2026.
Extends eligible expenditures for the regional opportunities investment tax credit to before January 1, 2027.
Updates rules for the Ontario Trillium Benefit and the small beer manufacturers' tax credit.
Caps secondary market ticket resale price at the original purchase price plus fees, service charges and taxes.
Bars secondary sellers from charging extra fees if the platform operator already charges one.
Requires proof of original ticket price before a platform can facilitate its resale.
States no one is entitled to compensation resulting from this Schedule or its regulations.
Sets board membership at 7 to 9 appointees by the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
Requires over half of members to come from an advisory committee's recommendations to the Minister.
Sets rules on the advisory committee's composition and recommendation criteria.
Changes rules on building construction, planning, transit fares, and water services across multiple Ontario laws.
Aims to speed up housing and infrastructure development and improve transit fare coordination across the province.
Clarifies environmental protection standards count as construction/demolition by-laws under section 35.
Makes matching clarifications in the City of Toronto Act and Planning Act on construction standards.
Repeals municipal by-law powers on environmental protection and conservation in two other Acts.
Removes references to "sustainable design" from section 114.
Bars Toronto from requiring electric vehicle charging equipment in parking facilities.
Prevents Toronto from imposing requirements on prescribed matters despite subsection (11).
Exempts non-profit retirement home developments from development charges under new section 4.5.
Makes small technical corrections to cross-references.

a.t: Fare Alignment and Seamless Transit Act, 2026
p: Lets the Minister set fare structures, discounts and transfer policies for prescribed transit systems.
Requires prescribed systems to join a unified fare payment system approved by the Minister.
Allows designation of fare zones and priority routes with service standards.
Requires specialized transit systems for persons with disabilities to join a unified trip booking system.
Creates a process for Metrolinx to notify chief building officials about building work on transit projects.
Sets rules for inspections, occupancy opinions, and reporting by chief building officials.
Grants immunity to officials acting in good faith and extinguishes a related cause of action.
Requires municipal consent before constructing or operating a water or sewage public utility.
Requires municipalities to grant consent if criteria set by regulation are met.
Adds new regulation-making powers for the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
Lets the County of Simcoe become an upper-tier municipality without planning powers at staggered times.
Removes requirement for official plans to address greenhouse gas mitigation and climate adaptation.
Bars zoning by-laws from requiring electric vehicle charging equipment at parking facilities.
Limits municipalities' ability to set minimum lot sizes above prescribed area for urban residential land.
Expands the definition of municipal drinking water system to include water and wastewater public corporations.
Adds new deemed consent provisions under section 53.

a.t: Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025
p: Restricts share ownership of water and wastewater public corporations to governments and their agents.
Requires board resolution before transferring assets used for water and sewage services.
Sets continuity of employment rules for staff transferred to these corporations.
Gives the Minister power to regulate the legal effect of asset transfers and related agreements.
Gives the Chief Electoral Officer, not Cabinet, power to appoint returning officers for each electoral district
Allows polling day to fall between the 36th and 42nd day after the writ, instead of a fixed date
Removes previous powers to recommend or choose an alternate polling day
Requires political ads generated wholly or partly by artificial intelligence to state this fact
Bans knowingly transmitting or publishing false or misleading content on candidate eligibility, election dates, polling locations or results
Lets the Chief Electoral Officer order removal or destruction of non-compliant transmissions or publications within 12 hours
Non-compliance with such a removal direction can lead to an administrative monetary penalty
Changes how some regional and upper-tier municipal councils in Ontario are structured and appointed, starting after the 2026 election.
Adjusts election rules so certain nominations for head of council and Niagara Region seats are treated as withdrawn for the 2026 election.
Changes timing rules for regional municipalities reviewing lower-tier council representation.
Lets the Minister regulate voting by upper-tier council members after the 2026 election.
Sets new rules and regulation powers for appointing heads of council after 2026.
Creates council composition rules for Simcoe, Niagara, Thorold, Port Colborne and Niagara-on-the-Lake.
Deems certain 2026 nominations for head of council and Niagara Region seats withdrawn.
Gives regulation-making power for running the 2026 election in these municipalities.
This section only applies if the Bill gets Royal Assent on or after May 1, 2026.
Changes decision-making and oversight in Ontario's education system, expanding the Minister's powers over school boards, child care, and post-secondary accreditation
Replaces existing bodies (Languages of Instruction Commission, OCSTA/OPSBA as bargaining agents) with new arrangements and eventually dissolves the Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario

a.t: Child Care and Early Years Act, 2014
p: Minister gets added power to support operators and service system managers
Minister may assign an Ontario education number to a child at parent's request
Minister gains power to set policies on student assessment, board expenses, materials, and communications
Repeals Minister's power over school climate surveys and boards' related reporting duty
Boards must get Minister's approval to acquire land, expropriate, or alter/repair school buildings
Minister may direct or replace board control over building projects and require fee payment

a.t: Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario Act, 2005
p: Changes composition and appointment rules for the Council's board, some deemed Minister-appointed
New provisions wind up and dissolve the Council, Minister prepares its final annual report
Act itself is to be repealed on a future date set by the Lieutenant Governor in Council
Splits regulation power over teacher education program accreditation from ongoing education program accreditation
New accreditation rules for teacher education can override post-secondary institutions' academic authority
Replaces OCSTA and OPSBA with the Council of Ontario Directors of Education (CODE) as employer bargaining agency
New CODE oversight committee governs bargaining process, rules may be set by Minister or by-law
Minister may replace CODE as bargaining agent if CODE is unable or unwilling to act
OCSTA may observe central bargaining and can shift matters to local bargaining affecting denominational rights
Amends the Health Protection and Promotion Act to add colon cancer screening rules
Requires every board of health to ensure colon cancer screening is available
Screening must include colonoscopies for people aged 45 and older
Takes effect three months after receiving Royal Assent
Short title is the Bishop Brigante Colon Cancer Prevention Act, 2026
Removes the rent control exemption for certain units, ending the vacancy decontrol exception in section 6.1
Requires termination notices for demolition, conversion or repair to include approvals and engineer documentation proving vacant possession is needed
Requires landlords ending a tenancy for repairs to offer a comparable unit or pay compensation up to 15 per cent above former rent or 30 per cent above median market rent
Ties new tenants' lawful rent to the amount previously charged for the unit, ending rent reset on turnover
Creates a rent registry run by the Landlord and Tenant Board requiring landlords to file rent statements within 30 days of a lease
Establishes a Rental Task Force to study above-guideline rent increases and publish a report within six months
Bars municipal approval of conversions or demolitions losing six or more rental units unless rents are already above mid-range or replacement units and tenant relocation plans are provided
Bans businesses from using personalized algorithmic pricing to change prices for individual consumers
Personalized pricing means setting prices based on a consumer's data, like browsing history, location or income
Electronic shelf labels showing different prices based on personal data are named as an unfair practice
Online platforms charging different prices to consumers based on personal data are also banned
Changes apply to both the Consumer Protection Act, 2002 and the Consumer Protection Act, 2023
Rules take effect six months after the bill receives Royal Assent
The short title of this bill is the Fair Grocery Prices Act, 2026
A multi-part bill changing rules on workplace protections, environmental assessments, health workforce access, talent agencies, and workers' compensation benefits.
It also adjusts labour relations timelines, oversight of retirement homes, and qualification requirements for the Ombudsman.
Bans employers from charging employees for uniforms or other prescribed items, with limited exceptions.
Improperly charged amounts become enforceable as wages owing to the employee.
Director gains power to assign or refuse to assign certain complaints for investigation or inspection.
Money collected in enforcement must pay employees first, then be split among collector, Director and Minister.
Allows prescribing of approved class environmental assessments under re-enacted section 15.
For multi-proponent Part II.3 projects, one proponent's application is now sufficient.
Repeals ministry review requirement and ability to request Tribunal referral for applications.
Removes need for Lieutenant Governor in Council approval of Minister's decisions, though Minister may still refer.
Shortens construction-industry timelines from two months to one month for union certification applications.
Also shortens to one month the timeline for declaring a union no longer represents a bargaining unit.

a.t: Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care Act
p: Adds power to regulate admission of foreign medical school graduates to Ontario residency programs.
Allows rules prioritizing graduates with a connection to Ontario, with that connection to be defined by regulation.
Lets the Chief Prevention Officer collect personal data on workers' exposure to hazardous agents for a registry.
Allows Minister to recognize equivalent training and equipment standards from other Canadian jurisdictions.
Authorizes reimbursement to prescribed employers and constructors for cost of prescribed protective headwear.
Requires the Ombudsman appointee to be proficient in both English and French.
Requires unanimous selection by an all-party legislative panel chaired by the Speaker, unless the Assembly agrees otherwise.
Transfers authority to appoint directors of the Retirement Homes Regulatory Authority board from Cabinet to the Minister.
Minister must set appointment terms, and director appointees serve at the Minister's pleasure.
Updates mandatory-reporting category list, removing reference to repealed Drugless Practitioners Act practitioners.
Allows regulations to add further categories of persons required to report suspected incidents.
Creates a new Act banning talent agencies from charging entertainment workers fees beyond prescribed commissions.
Requires agencies to deposit client funds in dedicated accounts and remit payments within set timelines.
Establishes a Director of Talent Agencies with inspection, investigation, and order-making powers.
Sets up complaint processes, Ontario Labour Relations Board reviews, offences and penalties for violations.
Allows Board to pay benefits to workers past age 65 in certain determined circumstances.
Raises loss of earnings benefit rate from 85 per cent to 90 per cent of net earnings difference.
Applies similar benefit-rate increases to survivor's benefits.
Lets Board review long-standing loss of earnings payments after 72 months under new rules, without prior time limit.
Proclaims the last full week of May each year as Developmental Disabilities Awareness Week
Encourages all Ontarians to wear something yellow during that week
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Developmental Disabilities Awareness Week Act, 2026
Bans operators of electronic gaming sites from advertising or promoting the site or anything offered on it
Exempts foreign publications, artistic works and news commentary that don't promote gambling for payment
Sets fines up to $100,000 for individuals and $1,000,000 for corporations who break the advertising ban
Requires the Registrar to revoke a supplier's registration after a second or subsequent conviction
Cites rising ConnexOntario helpline calls and youth gambling harms since online gambling privatization in 2022
Takes effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Requires newly elected members of Ontario's Legislative Assembly to take an oath or affirmation of office
Members must swear before the Clerk of the Assembly before sitting or voting for the first time
Oath includes promises to act with fairness, integrity, honesty and impartiality
Members must pledge not to accept payment or reward for biased or corrupt conduct
Oath commits members to represent constituents and act in the public interest
Members who do not take the oath are not entitled to take their seat
Applies to members elected on or after the next general election after the law takes effect

A wide-ranging agriculture bill that restructures oversight of beef, milk and food safety rules, creates a new farmland ownership restriction, and updates tribunals, food dealer protections and veterinary regulation.
Producers providing cattle for custom processing must hold a licence, or are deemed to hold one
Producers processing their own cattle must pay prescribed licence fees as if cattle were sold
Producers can seek reimbursement of licence fees for up to two head processed for personal use
Repeals sections 10-16, removing carcass-weight purchase rules and related hearing/appeal processes

a.t: Farming and Food Production Protection Act, 1998
p: Transfers powers and duties of the Normal Farm Practices Protection Board to the Agriculture and Agri-Food Protection Tribunal
Makes other amendments, including transitional rules, to reflect this transfer
Prohibits designated persons, including foreign nationals or certain entities, from purchasing or acquiring farmland
Regulations may create exemptions from the prohibition
Requires conveyance information to be given to the Minister; registrars must refuse registration if missing
Sets up permission applications, inspectors, investigators, compliance orders and offences
Expands the Act's scope to cover milk and milk products
Updates administrative penalty rules in re-enacted section 41 and new sections 41.1 and 41.2
Re-enacts Part VI with new rules on delegated authorities, replacing former section 49
Replaces Crown liability rules in section 50 and adds new section 50.1 on delegated authority liability
Adds milk products to the definition of 'regulated product' and updates references from cream/cheese
Removes the Act's role in regulating the quality of milk and milk products
Removes the Act's governance of plants
Adds new inspection powers in re-enacted sections 8 and 9, and new transition regulation authority in section 26.1

a.t: Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs Act
p: Renames the Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs Appeal Tribunal as the Agriculture and Agri-Food Protection Tribunal
Extends the deadline for the Tribunal to send decisions and reasons from 20 to 30 days after a hearing
Applies the new 30-day period transitionally to hearings already completed before the amendment's effective date
Makes French-version amendments for consistency with the English text
Declares the Ontario Food Terminal Board an agent of the Crown in right of Ontario
Allows reserve funds under section 7 to include capital funds
Adds liability protections for the Crown, its employees/agents, and Board members, officers, employees and the manager

a.t: Protecting Farmers from Non-Payment Act (Regulating Agricultural Product Dealers and Storage Operators), 2023
p: Repeals and replaces the definition of 'dealer'
Extends agreement rules to cover prescribed buyers and sellers, not just dealers and producers
Updates storage operator rules on weigh tickets, storage receipts and shortfall permits
Adds new Part VII.1 setting rules for collection and grading of designated agricultural products
Adds a definition of 'ancillary services' and revises the definition of 'Minister'
Creates exceptions to the certificate of accreditation requirement in new subsections 21(3) and (4)
Amends rules on members who knew or should have known licence application information was false
Expands entry and inspection powers for veterinary facilities and other prescribed premises
Lets the Minister of Transportation take specific City of Toronto lands near Billy Bishop Airport and vest them in the Crown
Buildings, structures, fixtures and improvements owned by the City on that land also transfer to the Crown automatically
Bans the City from selling, encumbering or disposing of these lands or assets, making any such deals void
Requires the Crown to pay the City compensation based on market value from official appraisal reports
Sends compensation disputes to binding arbitration instead of the courts
Replaces the City with the Crown as a party to the 1983 Tripartite Agreement on airport operations
Blocks most lawsuits against the Crown over this Act and states the changes are not legal expropriation
Declares April of each year as Nepali Heritage Month in Ontario
Recognizes contributions of Nepali Ontarians to the province's political, social, economic and cultural life
Notes Nepali immigration to Canada began after diplomatic relations started in 1965
Highlights significant Nepali communities in Greater Toronto Area, Ottawa, London, Windsor, Hamilton, Guelph and Kitchener-Waterloo
References Nepali festivals like Dashain, Tihar and Teej and the Bikram Samvat calendar
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title given is the Nepali Heritage Month Act, 2026
Creates Lydia's Law focused on accountability in handling sexual assault cases
Requires the Attorney General to publish a yearly progress report on implementing 2019 Auditor General recommendations
Progress report must go to the Assembly by March 1 each year and online within 10 days
Standing Committee on Justice Policy must set up a working group to review each progress report
Attorney General must review efficiency of the Victim Quick Response Program and report within one year
Police services must tell sexual assault complainants aged 16 or older about the Independent Legal Advice Program
Removes time limits on regulatory bodies' funding for mental health support for alleged sexual abuse victims
Requires Ontario to develop a food affordability plan within 12 months of the Act coming into force
Plan must be published on a Government of Ontario website
Requires new legislation to void restrictive covenants and exclusivity clauses limiting competition among food retailers
Requires prohibiting such property controls and imposing penalties for violations
Requires municipal consultation when developing this new legislation
Requires the Minister of Finance to take steps toward removing HST on food products and non-alcoholic beverages
Includes amending provincial law and seeking federal agreement to remove tax on groceries
Lets Ontario's Minister create regulations giving credits or payments for part of the federal HST paid on residential property
Caps each credit or payment at $50,000 per person
Requires that any purchase agreement deadline for eligibility be no later than March 31, 2027
Allows the federal minister or a supplier to issue the credit or payment on Ontario's behalf
Lets a person entitled to a payment assign it to someone else
Requires repayment if someone receives a credit or payment they were not entitled to
Makes both parties liable to repay if an assigned payment turns out to be undue
Creates the Black Health Equity Act, recognizing Black residents' right to equitable, culturally safe, anti-racist healthcare
Requires Ministry of Health to build a Black Health Equity Framework with annual racial equity audits and enforceable accountability measures
Requires public health units to create action plans, hire Black Health Equity Officers, and track racial disparities in care access
Requires hospitals and health units to set up Black-led Patient Advocacy and Protection Units and collect race-based data publicly
Establishes a Black Health Equity Council with oversight authority to review government budgets, policies and legislation
Creates a Black Health Equity Inspectorate to investigate racial harm and impose funding consequences for non-compliance
Requires a plan for fully covering culturally responsive mental health services and a system of reparative justice for survivors of anti-Black racism
Requires the Minister to create a timed plan to bring into force the Correctional Services Transformation Act, 2018 schedules within six months
Adds whistle-blower protections for people reporting alleged contraventions of prescribed correctional services laws
Bans reprisals like firing, demotion, discipline or intimidation against whistle-blowers, with fines and civil remedies
Voids confidentiality agreement clauses that try to stop whistle-blowing, cooperation with investigations or giving evidence
Lets courts or arbitrators order reinstatement, double back pay, or other compensation for whistle-blowers facing reprisals
Gives the Inspector General power to compel correctional managers and certain ministers to provide safety and workplace information
Requires public online reporting of resident numbers at correctional institutions, updated at least every two months
Requires the Minister of Health to examine creating a grant program for travel costs to access specialist care
Grants would help Ontarians who must travel for medical specialist services unavailable locally
Eligibility includes being an Ontario resident referred by a primary care clinician for specialist care
Applicants must travel at least 100 kilometres one-way to reach the nearest needed specialist or facility
Travel costs must not already be covered by programs like WSIB, federal Non-Insured Health Benefits, or private insurance
Applications must be made within 12 months of treatment, with original receipts provided
Minister must table a report within six months describing steps to fully fund the program within a further six months
Declares May of every year as Buddhist Heritage Month in Ontario
Recognizes Buddhism's role in Ontario's spiritual and cultural life
Notes over 300,000 Buddhists in Canada, more than half living in Ontario
References Vesak, a May observance marking Buddha's birth, enlightenment and Nirvana
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Buddhist Heritage Month Act, 2026
A wide-ranging justice and public-safety bill that changes adoption rules, policing oversight, sex offender registry rules, human trafficking debt protections, and several other Acts.
It creates two new laws (on restraining orders from other provinces and on pill presses/precursors) and amends 14 existing Acts covering policing, licensing, and victim protections.

a.t: Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
p: Lets a Director approve people as adoption practitioners to prepare homestudies and adjustment reports.
Allows licensees to bring foreign children into Ontario for adoption under a new licence term.
Director may refuse such a licence term if contrary to the public interest.
Allows locking a young person in a room in secure custody under prescribed rules.
Applies the Act to anyone subject to an order/obligation under the federal Sex Offender Information Registration Act.
Reporting duties last as long as the person is a sex offender under federal law.
Removes rules on pardons/overturned convictions; adds rules for destroying registry information.
Updates references from 'the ministry' to 'the Minister' and other technical fixes.
Expands misconduct/complaint rules to cover prescribed persons beyond police officers.
Gives the Minister power to issue directives setting priorities for police service boards.
Requires public disclosure of certain personal information by the Commissioner on a website.
Lets out-of-province officers, like RCMP, exercise prescribed police powers in Ontario.

a.t: Enforcement of Canadian Restraining Orders Act, 2026
p: New Act makes restraining orders from other Canadian courts enforceable as Ontario orders.
Such orders can be registered with an Ontario court.
Parties can apply to vary or set aside a non-Ontario restraining order under specified conditions.
Applications to leave Ontario for adoption may now only go through a licensee, not a Director.
Directors may approve adoption practitioners and require corrective directions from them.
New licence terms let licensees facilitate adoptions from specific countries, subject to public-interest refusal.
Adds binding directives and compliance orders for licensees who break the rules.
New Act defines and restricts use, possession or sale of pill presses and precursor chemicals.
Prohibits possessing proceeds from offences under the Act and requires reporting stolen pill presses.
Lets police demand identification from suspects and sets out search, seizure and penalty rules.
Lets municipalities impose administrative penalties for violations of land-use restriction by-laws.
Unpaid penalties become a debt collectible like municipal taxes if not paid within 15 days.
Lets a chief of police apply to the Minister to have a body designated as an 'authorized body' under federal law.
Minister may make regulations governing this designation process.

a.t: Prevention of and Remedies for Human Trafficking Act, 2017
p: Re-enacts rules letting trafficking victims establish and stop collection of coerced debts.
Creditors must pause debt collection once a designated organization confirms a debt is coerced.
Sets up simplified adjudicator process, alongside courts, to decide contested coerced debt claims.
Repeals the 2023 coerced-debts Act, folding its substance into this Act.

a.t: Private Security and Investigative Services Act, 2005
p: Redefines security guard work as guarding and patrolling, not just guarding or patrolling.
Minister, not Lieutenant Governor in Council, now appoints the Registrar and deputy registrars.
Paying licence fees becomes mandatory for licence eligibility.
Justices of the peace can now issue production orders to investigators.
Extends existing dog record-keeping requirement to also cover cats and other prescribed animals.
Creates a process for court clerks to enter guilty pleas and fines agreed between defendant and prosecutor.
Cases proceed to trial before a justice if agreement requirements aren't met.
Re-enacts the definition of 'court' to expressly include a justice, with consequential changes.

a.t: Social Work and Social Service Work Act, 1998
p: Allows interim suspension or conditions on a member's certificate as soon as a complaint or investigation begins, not only after referral to a hearing.
Allows more people to be prescribed as 'officials' under the Act.
Lets the SIU Director refer certain matters to a prescribed person, not just a chief of police.

a.t: Towing and Storage Safety and Enforcement Act, 2021
p: Further appeals no longer automatically stay a decision unless the Divisional Court orders it.
Bans providing or offering towing services within 200 metres of a collision.
Also bans tow trucks from parking or stopping within 200 metres of a collision.
Lets the Director delegate powers to Ministry employees.
Adds victims of criminal harassment to those presumed to have suffered emotional distress.
Creates a new civil cause of action for harassment, even without a criminal charge or conviction.
Courts must account for damages already awarded when a victim brings multiple harassment claims against the same person.
Declares the week starting May 1 each year as Ethnic Media and Community Media Appreciation Week
Recognizes ethnic media outlets operating in languages other than English and French
Acknowledges community media outlets covering local issues and neighbourhood events
Preamble notes these outlets help inform diverse and local communities about public affairs
Law takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Ethnic Media and Community Media Appreciation Week Act, 2026
Requires naloxone kits to be installed anywhere a defibrillator is required or voluntarily installed
Allows regulations to designate other publicly accessible places as needing naloxone kits
Owners must ensure kits are accessible, clearly signed, maintained, tested and staff trained
Naloxone kits must be registered with a designated registrar within 30 days of installation
Registrar must notify prescribed persons when kits are registered, moved or removed
Inspectors can enter non-dwelling premises without warrant to check compliance
Violations, obstruction or giving false information to inspectors can lead to prescribed fines
Proclaims the first full week of December each year as Romanian Heritage Week in Ontario
Recognizes contributions of Ontario's approximately 150,000 Romanian Canadians
Honours Romanian Canadian community achievements in entrepreneurship, education, athletics, arts, science and public service
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title given is the Romanian Heritage Week Act, 2026
Requires school boards to keep school buildings no hotter than 26 degrees Celsius when people are present
Requires school buses to be kept at no more than 26 degrees Celsius while operating
Boards must create and annually update a heat mitigation strategy for each school, with input from Joint Health and Safety Committees
Heat mitigation strategies must cover cooling systems, building adaptations, passive cooling and guidance on spotting heat stress
Boards must develop and update an emergency plan for extreme temperature events, including communication and evacuation steps
Minister of Education must review boards' heat strategies, identify gaps and inequities, and issue public reports at least every three years
Law takes effect one year after receiving Royal Assent
Declares the week starting the third Monday in February each year as Mining Awareness Week
States mining contributes significant economic benefits to Ontario
Aims to raise awareness of mining projects, value, careers and innovation
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Mining Awareness Week Act, 2026
Raises the minimum age to buy tobacco, vapour products or prescribed products from 19 to 21 years old
Bans all promotion of vapour products in any manner
Prohibits selling flavoured vapour products unless the flavour is tobacco-flavoured, and caps nicotine content
Limits vapour product sales to approved specialty vape stores or designated stores in remote or rural areas
Bans all online sales of vapour products
Requires local boards of health to approve and can revoke specialty vape store and remote store operations, barring anyone under 21 inside
Requires Ontario Health to issue an annual report on youth vaping to guide government policy
Amends the Land Titles Act to address notices of lodgement of title on property records
Deems all existing notices of lodgement of title expired on the day the Act takes effect
Requires the land registrar to delete all expired notices from the register within six months
States such notices have been used to manipulate homeowners and commit fraud
The Act is called the Protecting Homeowners from Title Fraud Act, 2026
Comes into force on the day it receives Royal Assent
Amends the Taxation Act, 2007 to reduce income tax for young individuals
Sets the lowest income tax rate amount to $0 for individuals under age 27
Applies to taxation years ending after December 31, 2026
Age is determined as of the first day of the taxation year
The tax exception automatically repeals five years after Royal Assent unless the Assembly renews it
The Assembly must pass a new resolution every five years to keep the exception in force
Known as the Fair Start for Young Workers Act, 2026
Adds cooling to the list of 'vital services' landlords must provide under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006
Requires room temperature to stay at most 26 degrees Celsius from June 1 to September 30 each year
Cooling requirement is considered met if a tenant can control the temperature to 26 degrees but chooses not to
Allows the government to make transition regulations to manage issues arising from these changes
The cooling requirement (Section 1) only takes effect on the later of January 1, 2035 or Royal Assent
Other parts of the Act come into force upon Royal Assent
Short title of the bill is the Hot Days, Cool Homes Act, 2026
Creates Andre's Law, adding a Residents' Bill of Rights for people living in supported group living residences
Guarantees rights to respect, dignity, freedom from abuse and neglect, and quality of life for residents
Grants rights to quality care, self-determination, informed decision-making, and privacy in personal care
Gives residents rights to security of tenure, complaints processes, and protection from eviction without Landlord and Tenant Board order
Allows creation of Residents' Councils and Family Councils to advise, resolve disputes, and improve care quality
Requires service agencies to consult with these Councils at least every three months and respond to concerns within 10 days
Lets the Lieutenant Governor in Council make regulations on how these rights and Council duties are carried out
Sets up new worker heat-stress protections and creates two new climate-related programs: a provincial climate adaptation strategy and an urban wildfire advisory process.
Adds a new Part IV.1 requiring the Minister to create a Worker Heat Protection Standard.
Employers must provide heat stress training to employees.
Employees must be paid regular wages for rest, breaks, medical removal and training time under the standard.
For 5 years, the Minister must annually report heat stress illness, deaths and enforcement to the Legislature.

a.t: Ontario Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience Act, 2026
p: Requires the Minister to develop and publish a strategic action plan protecting people, communities, infrastructure and nature from climate change risks.
Creates an arm's length Ontario Climate Adaptation Fund to support adaptation and resilience activities.
Establishes the Ontario Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience Resource Centre.
Requires a Whole-of-Government Climate Adaptation Co-ordination Secretariat to coordinate climate plans across all ministries and agencies.

a.t: Protecting Ontario from Urban Wildfires Act, 2026
p: Requires the Minister to establish an Urban Wildfires Advisory Committee within 90 days of the Act coming into force.
Committee must assess growing urban wildfire risks and timelines for increased risk levels.
Committee must recommend measures for prevention, suppression, recovery and public protection, reporting within one year.
Minister must then develop plans, legislation, and cooperation protocols between urban and forest wildfire forces.
Declares May 28 each year as Menstrual Health Day in Ontario
Aims to raise awareness of challenges faced by people who menstruate
Preamble notes menstrual products are often unaffordable, especially in Northern and Indigenous communities
Preamble links lack of access to health risks like toxic shock syndrome and sepsis
Intends to reduce stigma and normalize menstruation as a natural bodily function
Act takes effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Requires the Minister of Health to develop a paediatric hospice palliative care strategy for Ontario
Strategy aims to create equity of access to high quality paediatric hospice palliative care
Strategy must include targeted supports for families, including mental health supports
Minister must publish a report setting out the strategy within one year of Royal Assent
Creates a Paediatric Hospice Palliative Care Advisory Committee of 5 to 9 members
Committee includes health professionals and family members, with representation from five named cities
Committee reviews a 2011 work group report and gives yearly recommendations to the Minister
Requires the Minister of Health to publish a health care worker support strategy within six months of Royal Assent
Strategy must include workforce data collection, annual worker surveys on burnout and safety, and staffing action plans
Includes a timeline for a government apology over the 2019 wage-limiting law and reaffirming collective bargaining rights
Creates new honours, including an Exemplary Service Award and a Distinguished Conduct Medal, and a Health Professionals' Week in June
Sets out plans for wage parity, competitive pay, mental health supports, and workplace safety standards for health care workers
Imposes a financial penalty on the Minister and Premier personally if strategy deadlines are missed, equal to 10 per cent of their salary
Amends the Public Hospitals Act to extend maximum hospital medical staff appointments from one year to three years
Requires the Minister to create a working group within 60 days to review organic waste diversion from landfills
Working group must have at least 11 members including waste experts and industry representatives
Working group examines organic waste quantities, greenhouse gas emissions, and successful diversion strategies from other jurisdictions
Working group must report findings and recommended goals to the Minister within six months
Minister must table the report in the Legislature and publish it within 15 days of receiving it
Minister must respond to the report within three months and publish that response
Minister must publish annual public reports on organic waste in landfills, including quantities, emissions, and reduction plans
Proclaims July of each year as Swahili Heritage Month in Ontario
Honours Ontario's Swahili speakers and their contributions to culture and community
Date aligns with UNESCO's World Swahili Language Day, celebrated July 7
Act takes effect the day it receives Royal Assent
Bans leaving promotional materials visibly at private homes, with some exceptions
Promotional materials include flyers, brochures, leaflets, catalogues and similar items
Allows materials from municipal, provincial or federal politicians' constituency offices
Permits election materials from candidates or registered parties only during election periods, if no mailbox exists
Exempts materials distributed by the Ontario or Canadian governments
Does not apply to Canada Post employees or agents delivering mail
Takes effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Creates the Keeping Our Kids Safe Online Act, 2026, requiring the Minister to set up an Online Safety Advisory Committee within 60 days
Committee must include parents, youths, education workers, school board members and social media experts
Committee will study other jurisdictions and develop a plan to ban social media and AI chatbots in schools, with possible accessibility exceptions
Committee must create K-12 curricula on digital citizenship, online safety and artificial intelligence literacy, including misinformation, mental health and environmental harms
Committee must recommend ways to hold tech and social media companies accountable for harms like gambling, pornography, trafficking and misinformation
Committee must recommend funding and training for children's mental health organizations to address technology addiction

Minister must report to the Assembly and publish annual public reports on progress implementing the recommendations, and must use the Committee's curricula when setting Education Act curriculum guidelines
Requires the Minister of Health to create a written plan restricting social media use for people under 16
Plan must include a strategy to work with the federal government to ban social media for under-16s
Plan must set Ontario policies and timelines to enforce social media age restrictions
Plan must include policies for monitoring social media providers' compliance with age rules
Minister must consult the Minister of Education, the federal Health Minister, school boards, councils and teachers
Minister must table the plan in the Legislative Assembly within one year of the section taking effect
Minister must ensure the plan is implemented according to its own timelines
Requires the Minister to collect yearly data on housing units built, including bedroom mix and price ranges in $50,000 increments
Requires the data to be published on a government website within 90 days after each year ends
Requires official plans to allow up to four residential units in detached, semi-detached houses or rowhouses, and buildings up to four storeys
Requires official plans in larger municipalities to allow six to 11 storey midrise housing on major streets and transit corridors, if servicing capacity exists
Removes most rights to appeal these new housing policies, except appeals brought by the Minister
Bans official plans and by-laws from blocking four or fewer units, imposing minimum lot sizes, or limiting buildings to four storeys or less
Bans requiring parking spaces for buildings with four or more units and bans minimum setback rules for four to six unit buildings
Revives the dissolved corporation 1976998 Ontario Inc. by special legislation
Corporation was voluntarily dissolved under the Business Corporations Act on July 26, 2023
Application made by Bijun Gong and Zhenyu Gong, former directors and shareholders
Restores the corporation's property, rights, privileges and liabilities as if never dissolved
Purpose is to allow the corporation to carry on business again under its name
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives MFIS Holdings and Investments Inc, a corporation dissolved on February 11, 2020
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and franchises as if never dissolved
Restores all its liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from the dissolution date
Applicant Mohammed Shanshal was the corporation's sole director and president before dissolution
Revival allows the corporation to deal with real property still registered in its name
New rights acquired by other people after the dissolution remain protected
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives Gilda Investments Limited, a corporation dissolved on January 21, 1995
Corporation was dissolved for failing to comply with the Corporations Information Act
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and franchises as of its dissolution date
Also restores all its liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from that date
Revival is subject to any rights acquired by others after the dissolution
Application made by Gilda Lucy Price, executor of her late mother's estate
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent

Restores the company to its legal position as if never dissolved
Applicant Joel E. Marion was a director and shareholder before dissolution
Revival allows dealing with real property still held in the company's name
Rights acquired by others after dissolution remain protected
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives Social Asset Measurements Inc., a company dissolved on October 1, 2024
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and franchises as if never dissolved
Also restores the company's liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from the dissolution date
Revival is subject to any rights acquired by other people after the dissolution
Was requested by Anshula Chowdhury, the company's director at time of dissolution, to address outstanding liabilities
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives Andrew Zawadowski Medicine Professional Corporation, which was dissolved on December 19, 2024
Restores the corporation to its legal position as if it had never been dissolved
Reinstates all property, rights, privileges and franchises the corporation had before dissolution
Reinstates the corporation's liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts as of its dissolution date
Protects any rights acquired by other people after the corporation's dissolution
Takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives the dissolved company 2512681 Ontario Inc. under special legislation
Company was dissolved on June 21, 2024 under the Business Corporations Act
Applicant Gabriel Nussbaum was director and sole shareholder before dissolution
Revival allows the corporation to participate in legal proceedings
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and liabilities as if never dissolved
Restoration is subject to rights acquired by others after the dissolution
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives Thistletown Lions Club, a corporation dissolved on October 6, 2009

Restores the club's property, rights, privileges and franchises as they existed before dissolution
Also restores the club's liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from that time
Restoration does not affect rights acquired by others after the dissolution
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives Holy Trinity Restaurant Inc., a corporation dissolved voluntarily on September 26, 2024
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and franchises as if never dissolved
Also restores its liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from the dissolution date
Sole director and shareholder Marie Cormier sought revival to participate in legal proceedings
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Rights acquired by others after the dissolution remain protected
Revives Five Senses Productions Inc., a corporation dissolved on May 12, 2016
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and franchises as they existed before dissolution
Also restores the company's liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from the dissolution date
Revival is subject to any rights acquired by other people after the dissolution
Applicants Jeremy Podeswa and Camelia Frieberg were shareholders and directors when the company dissolved
They sought this law to carry on business again under the corporation's name
Revives 1955274 Ontario Inc., a corporation dissolved on June 23, 2022
Restores the company's property, rights, privileges and franchises as if never dissolved
Company remains subject to its prior liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts
Revival is subject to any rights acquired by others after the dissolution
Applicant Antonio Valerio Henriques was the corporation's sole director at dissolution

Revives Faris Team Mortgage Brokerage Corp., a company dissolved on December 22, 2023
Restores the corporation's property, rights, privileges and franchises as if never dissolved
Also restores the corporation's liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts from the dissolution date
Revival is subject to any rights acquired by other people after the dissolution
Allows the sole director to deal with property still held in the corporation's name

Revives Jarm Holdings Investments Ltd., a corporation dissolved on November 22, 2012
Applicant Ancilio Domingos was a director of the corporation before dissolution
Revival aims to allow dealing with real property held in the corporation's name at dissolution
Corporation restored to its legal position, including property, rights and liabilities, as if never dissolved
Restoration is subject to any rights acquired by others after the dissolution
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives the dissolved company 2708634 Ontario Ltd. by special legislation
Company was voluntarily dissolved under the Business Corporations Act on June 10, 2022
Sole director and shareholder Paula Silver applied to revive it
Revival lets her deal with real property held in the company's name
Company is restored to its legal position, property, rights and liabilities as before dissolution
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives the dissolved company 1581766 Ontario Ltd. as a legal entity

Applicant Bhupinder Sarkaria was the sole director and officer at dissolution
Revival allows the company to deal with property still held in its name

Revives Ludger Michel Estates Limited, a corporation dissolved on March 24, 2021
Restores the company to its legal position as if never dissolved
Includes its property, rights, privileges and franchises upon revival
Also restores its liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts as of dissolution date
Revival is subject to any rights acquired by others after dissolution
Allows the applicant to collect monies owed to the corporation
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives the dissolved corporation 2163694 Ontario Ltd. through special legislation
Corporation was dissolved on September 19, 2024 under the Business Corporations Act
Applicant Denise Caron was the sole director and shareholder before dissolution
Revival allows dealing with property still held in the corporation's name
Restores the corporation's property, rights, privileges and liabilities as if never dissolved
Rights acquired by others after the dissolution remain protected
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Repeals the 1917 Act respecting The Friends' Seminary of Ontario, which incorporated Pickering College
Repeals The Pickering College Act, 1960-61, which had amended the 1917 Act
Passed at the request of Pickering College itself
Takes effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Sets the short title as the Pickering College Act, 2026
Revives the corporation 730159 Ontario Ltd., which was dissolved on June 11, 1994
Dissolution occurred for failing to comply with the Corporations Information Act
Applicant Rolf-Harro Cohrs says he was the sole director and the default was inadvertent
Corporation is restored to its legal position, including property, rights, privileges and franchises
Revived corporation remains subject to its prior liabilities, contracts, disabilities and debts
Restoration is subject to any rights acquired by others after the dissolution
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Revives the dissolved company 1000401924 Ontario Inc. through special legislation
The company was voluntarily dissolved under the Business Corporations Act on November 13, 2024
